The Venerable Fifth Patriarch Huineng’s biological father was originally from Fanyang. Having been demoted and exiled to Lingnan, he became a commoner in Xinzhou. This...
His life was unfortunate; his father died early, leaving his aged mother orphaned. He moved to the South Sea region, where he lived in hardship and poverty, selling firewood in the marketplace.
Once, a customer bought some wood and told him to deliver it to an inn.

After the customer had taken the wood, Huineng received the payment and stepped outside the gate, where he saw another customer reciting a scripture. Upon hearing the words of the scripture, Huineng’s mind was immediately opened.
Wu then asked the guest what scripture he was reciting. The guest replied, "The Diamond Sutra. He asked again, "Where have you come from to hold this scripture?
The guest said, "I have come from East Chan Temple in Huangmei County, Qizhou.
That temple is where the Great Master Wuzu Ren presided over the teachings; there are more than a thousand disciples there. I went there to pay my respects and listen to the Dharma."

Receive this sutra. The Great Master constantly exhorted both monastics and laypeople to simply uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, whereby they would directly perceive their own nature and immediately realize Buddhahood.
—The Sixth Patriarch Master.

The following day, Huineng’s master went secretly to the rice-pounding shed. Seeing Huineng with a stone around his waist pounding rice, he said, "One who seeks the Way for the sake of the Dharma forgets their own body;
should it be thus? He then asked, "Is the rice finished? Huineng replied, "The rice has long been finished; there is only a lack of sifting.
The master struck the pestle three times with his staff and departed. Huineng immediately understood his master's meaning.
At the third beat of the drum, he entered the room. The Patriarch surrounded him with his *kāṣāya* so that no one could see them, and for him he preached the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

When they reached the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling on anything," Huineng attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words. He realized that all phenomena do not depart from one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
He then addressed the Patriarch, saying: "How unexpected it is that my own nature is fundamentally pure! How unexpected it is that my own nature is fundamentally..."

"Arising and ceasing—how unexpected that the self-nature is fundamentally complete! How unexpected that the self-nature is fundamentally unmoving! How unexpected that the self-nature can give rise to the myriad dharmas!
The Patriarch, having realized his original nature, said to Huineng: "If you do not recognize your own fundamental mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit.
If you recognize your own fundamental mind and see your own original nature, you are then called a Great Man, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, and a Buddha."
(Also published: *The Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra*).
Great Master Mingjiao Song [Yun] initially traveled from Dongshan to Mount Kang, establishing his presence at the Dharma seat of Kaixian. The presiding master, regarding him...

Jia Shaonian was keenly devoted to literature, and [the Emperor] ordered him to serve as a secretary. Mingjiao laughed and said, "How could I do this for you for the sake of a single cup of ginger-pear soup?
Thereupon, he departed from him. He resided at West Lake in Hangzhou for thirty years, keeping his door closed and not engaging in frivolous social intercourse.

In the Jiayou era, he presented the *Fujiao bian* (Compilation on Aiding the Teaching), the *Dingzu tu* (Chart of the Fixed Patriarchs), and the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage) to the imperial court.
At that time, Wang Gong Su, the Hanlin Academician who was serving as the Acting Governor of Kaifeng, submitted a memorial of recommendation to the court.
Emperor Renzong marveled at it for a long time and sent the document down to the Chancellor, Duke Han, and the State Councilor, Duke Ou.

Upon reading his writings, they were greatly astonished and praised him among the officials and gentlemen of the court. The document was ultimately granted entry into the imperial canon, and Mingjiao’s fame consequently spread throughout the world.
In the evening, he moved his residence to the Yong’an Hermitage north of Lingyin. At dawn, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* without ceasing his voice.
After his midday meal, he read books. When guests arrived, they engaged in pure conversation that did not touch upon worldly affairs.

He once remarked: "When guests depart, pure conversation diminishes; as years advance, white hair abounds. At midnight, he would recite the name of Avalokiteśvara until he had completed one hundred thousand invocations.
Then he retired to his bed. His austere, rigorous, and frugal lifestyle was sufficient to rival that of Sengyuan of Mount Zhong.
I once saw a letter he had written by hand to Chan Master Yue, which said: "Over the past few years, I have wished to make a paper quilt to ward off the bitter cold;
now, fortunately, it is finished. I imagine you would laugh heartily upon hearing this. At the time of his death, he sat upright with a smile and requested—

He composed a verse with his brush, saying: "The moon is bright at the beginning of the late night; I shall now go forth alone. I do not emulate the old man of Dàméi, who still craved the cries of the flying squirrel.
After he passed away, they cremated him. His cranial bone, eyes, teeth, tongue, ears, brow-hairs, male organ, and prayer beads were all indestructible.
This was just as the World-Honored One had said: "A bhikṣu whose physical body does not decay emits the light of stainless wisdom."
By the power of the merit of his roots of goodness and the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, he maintained internal and external purity in every movement— whether walking,
standing, sitting, or reclining. It is an error to place Master [Xuefeng] within the lineage of Master Deshan Yuan as recorded in the *Zongpai tu* (Lineage Chart),
for he received the Dharma from Master Dongshan Cui (as noted in Hong Juefan’s *Linjian lu*).
Master Zhongfeng was a native of Hangzhou.

Having entered the order under a teacher to shave his head and receive full ordination, he resolved to investigate the Way, vowing not to rest until he had reached the inner sanctum of the ancient masters.
At that time, Master Gaofeng held the "contract" of Yangshan Xueyan and resided at Tian... (text fragment ends).
He visited Mushi Rock and established himself at the Barrier of Death, vowing never to receive a patch-robed monk. Upon seeing the Master [Mushi] for the first time, he was filled with great joy;

the Master bestowed upon him a *huatou* (critical phrase). The Master applied himself with diligent vigor to seek resolution, and while reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he reached the passage concerning "shouldering the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Tathāgata.
At that moment, he attained a sudden and thorough awakening. From then on, his wisdom and discernment became unimpeded, reaching even up to kings and ministers.
From the high ministers down to the eminent scholars of the Three Teachings, there were none who did not humble themselves to inquire after the Way.

His writings and recorded sayings, comprising several volumes, were collected by his disciple T’ien-ch’u and submitted to the imperial court for inclusion in the Great Canon. He was posthumously bestowed with the title of National Teacher Puying.

The Master’s physical frame was imposing and robust; whenever he slightly lowered his head, he would gasp for breath, so he habitually sat upright with eyes fixed straight ahead. Whenever anyone requested [instruction],...
Dharma Words. Written with a brush as they came, carried by two *dhūta* practitioners (from the *Chu-shan-an za-lu*).
Regarding Rui-xue-ya:
Rui-xue-ya was a native of Huang-yang. In his youth, he received ordination from Master Qiu-jiang Zhan and resided at Xincheng Mountain.

He resided at Liuying Monastery. He was strict and meticulous in observing the Vinaya rules and daily recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He was particularly skilled in the ritual practices of Yoga.

Whenever he was invited by monastics or laypeople, he always conducted himself with the utmost reverence; yet, regarding offerings and gifts, he did not discriminate between their abundance or meagerness.

Even when there were none at all, he paid them no mind. When invited again, he would attend just as before. In the fifth month of the summer of the Xinhai year of the Hongwu era, he fell slightly ill.
He fell ill. He requested hot water to bathe and changed his robes, then wrote a verse. Sitting cross-legged, he passed away.

During the cremation, sparks mixed with rays of light radiated out, yet there was no smoke or flame at all. A great many *śarīra* (relics) were obtained. He was eighty-three years old. (From the *Shan'an zalu*).
There was an elder from Mount Jing named Qingci, whose style name was Yixi. In his prime, he did not observe the precepts and was indiscriminate in what he ate and drank.
Reaching middle age, he reflected to himself: "How much longer can the lifespan of a human being in this world last? One day, the demon of impermanence will strike."
When death approached, he wondered how he might dispel it. He then gathered all his accumulated clothing and assets to construct a hall dedicated to Avalokiteśvara to the east of Puking Temple.

There, he cultivated pure deeds and prayed to be reborn in the Pure Land. After several years had passed, while copying the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* by hand, he reached the passage concerning the "three thousand great thousandfold worlds.
Grasping his pen, he straightened his body and sat upright, passing away. In the Zhizheng...
In the year of Dingyou, the Miao tribesmen set fire to Puqing Temple and the dwellings of the residents. Only the Hall of Guanyin remained standing tall and intact.
The Buddha taught that the retribution for good and evil is like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound; yet he did not believe this (from the *Shan'an zalu*).
In the winter of the Gengxu year of the Hongwu era, Tian Zizhong of Fenghua visited me at Taibai and stayed for a long time.

I happened to remark that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is called the "Sūtra of Merit" within the realm of King Yama; therefore, when people of the world offer it on behalf of the deceased...

He read it many times. Among his sons, he vowed to uphold it for the rest of his life. One day, coinciding with the anniversary of his mother’s death, he resolved to recite this sutra one hundred times as an offering for her.
As he sat upon a pine-wood couch at dawn and was reciting it for the ninth time, he saw a ghostly executioner with cangues and shackles and an old woman kneeling before the couch.
Her hair was disheveled and covered her face; looking closely, he realized it was his deceased mother.
Zi Zhong was suddenly overcome with distress, not knowing what to do. In a moment, he led her away as if she were being released from her shackles.

Thereupon, Zi Zhong wept bitterly, regretting that he had not immediately ceased his recitation of the sutra to inquire after his mother’s well-being. I say that the merit of this sutra is so great it cannot be adequately described.
Had Zi Zhong resolved his mind to uphold and recite it, there would have been a mystical response from the realm of the unseen, causing—
Mother and son were both able to see one another, thereby releasing them from their suffering. How magnificent! (From the *Shan'an Zalu*). Regarding the Spirit of Tinghu Lake:
On the banks of the Yangtze River in the Jin dynasty, there was the Spirit of Tinghu Lake, who was extremely stern and malevolent. At that time, there was a visiting monk... [text fragment ends]
There was a Brahmin named Dharmakara who was skilled at reciting mantras to ward off various malevolent poisons, all of which were proven effective.
A certain junior monk went to Dharmakara to study these mantras for several years; having completed his studies, he too was able to subdue various malevolent poisons and evils.
Consequently, he went to the shrine of the Tinghu spirit to stay the night, where he recited mantras to subjugate the deity. That night, he saw the spirit, and thus...
He lost his life. When the Master from Tibet heard that his disciple had recited the mantra to death, he was filled with resentment and came in person.

Arriving at the shrine at night, he recited the mantra with a wrathful intent. The deity appeared before him, and the Master himself also died. There was a monk in the same monastery who constantly maintained the practice of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Hearing that both the master and his disciple had perished, he went to the site of the deity. At night in the temple, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and when it reached the night...
Midway through, he heard a wind-like sound that was exceedingly great. In an instant, he saw a certain object;
its form was massive and towering, strikingly awe-inspiring, wondrous and terrifying. Its teeth were long and sharp, and its eyes flashed like lightning.

Its various supernatural transformations cannot be fully described. Yet the master of the sūtras sat upright in right mindfulness, reciting the scripture without a moment’s slackening, his mind free from fear.
He felt no anxiety or fear at all. The spirit perceived his tranquil countenance; setting aside its formidable power, it approached the Master.
It knelt with its right knee on the ground, joined its palms in reverence, and listened to the sutra until it was finished. The Master asked the spirit, "Donor, what kind of deity are you?
At first you were fierce and imposing, but now you appear composed and relaxed. The spirit replied, "Your disciple has received such a retribution for my evil karma. I am the deity of this lake."

Nevertheless, he was deeply faithful and respectful. The Master of the Sūtras asked again, "If you are so faithful and respectful, for what reason did you previously strike both masters until they died?
He replied, "The reason the previous two masters died was that they were unable to uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras; instead, they recited mantras with a mind of anger.
When they saw their disciples approaching, they met them head-on with insults, focusing solely on reciting evil words to subjugate them. The disciples..."
I prostrate. At that time, the two monks, seeing the disciple’s hideous appearance, were naturally struck with fear and died; it was not because the disciple intentionally killed them.
When the monastics and laypeople nearby saw the two monks had been killed, they assumed the Scripture Master had also died.

They gathered together to go and look, only to find him safe and sound, his countenance serene and composed. The people of the time were greatly astonished and vied with one another to ask for the reason. He answered them in detail as before.

I believe this is truly due to the power of Prajñā; the holy teaching is not in vain. Many people have, because of this, resolved their minds to receive and uphold the Prajñā (as recorded in the Collection of Hou Junsu).
Xiao Yu, Xiao Yu.

He was the great-grandson of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and the son of Prince Kui of Liang. After the fall of the Liang, he entered the Sui dynasty and served as Grand Secretary (Zhongshu Ling), being enfeoffed as the Duke of Anguo.
His daughter was the Empress of Emperor Yang. He was a devoted believer in the Buddha-dharma and constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. [End of] Discourse.

The campaign against Goguryeo did not accord with the Emperor’s wishes, and he was greatly incensed. He placed Yu together with He Ruo-bi and Gao Lü under house arrest, intending to execute them according to the law.
Yu went to their quarters and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* seven hundred times over eight days.

On the following day, his shackles suddenly fell off of their own accord. The guards were struck with alarm and hastily re-fastened them. When they arrived before the palace, the Emperor alone granted Yu clemency, while the other two were immediately severely punished. Consequently—
There are eighteen accounts of miraculous responses concerning the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He constructed a precious stupa to enshrine the scripture, made of sandalwood and three feet in height.
Moved by this, a brass image suddenly appeared in his courtyard; he enshrined it within the stupa and obtained one hundred grains of śarīra.
In the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, he saw the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra gradually departing toward the west (from the *Baoying ji*).

Zhao Wenruo was a native of Chang’an County in Yongzhou during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty. Seven days after his death, when his family was performing the major funeral rites and was about to place him in the coffin, he contracted one of his legs.
The family members were terrified and did not dare to put him in the coffin. Zhao Wenruo then...
Wenruo was revived. His kinsmen joyfully asked for the reason. Wenruo said: "At first, someone led me to the presence of the King.
The King asked me, 'During your lifetime, what meritorious deeds did you perform? Wenruo answered the King, 'I upheld the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
The King sighed in admiration, saying, 'Excellent! This merit is foremost. Although your merit is virtuous, nevertheless, I shall show you the place where you must undergo punishment.'"
He led Wenruo ten paces north until they reached a hole in a wall. He had Wenruo enter;
from within the wall, someone reached out a hand through the hole and seized Wenruo by the head, pulling him out. Having endured extreme hardship, he finally crossed to the outside of the wall.
There he saw the great hells with their boiling cauldrons and instruments of torture. The sufferings of the sinners were beyond description. Now there was...
A great multitude of pigs, sheep, chickens, ducks, and other such creatures came vying with one another to follow Wenruo, as if seeking their lives back from him in debt.

Wenruo said, "I do not eat your bodies; why do you press me so? The animals replied, "In the past, at such-and-such a place, you ate our heads, feet, and four limbs, tearing them apart joint by joint for each person to drink and devour. Why do you now deny it? Wenruo single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name, deeply...
He repented of his sins and uttered no further words, seeking only to cultivate merit as an act of atonement. The various animals each dispersed.
The man led Wenruo back to the king’s presence. The king gave him a bowl of nails and ordered Wenruo to eat them;

furthermore, he drove five nails into the crown of Wenruo’s head and into his hands and feet, and only then released him to return home. Wenruo regained consciousness and recounted these events in detail.
However, he suffered from headaches and ailments in his hands and feet. After practicing merit for a long time, his pain gradually subsided.

Since then, he has diligently recited and upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, not daring to waste even a moment. Whenever he saw monastics or laypeople, whether close or distant relatives, they all exhorted him to uphold it.
Later, while on an official mission, he stopped at a post station hall to rest for a short while. At that time, he dreamed of one...
A woman dressed in blue robes came in haste to beg for her life. Wenruo woke up in alarm and immediately summoned the station master, asking him, "Did you intend to kill a living being for my sake?
The station master replied, "Indeed, it was for your sake that I intended to kill a small sheep.
Wenruo asked, "What color is that sheep? He answered, "It is a blue ewe. Wenruo told him, "Release it at once!"
"I shall ransom and release him at his own value. This was truly due to the profound assistance of the power of *prajñā* responding to conditions (from the *Mingxiang ji*).
By Zhao Wenchang.
In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Zhao Wenchang, an assistant director of the Grand Treasury Bureau, suddenly died of a violent illness.

Only his heart remained slightly warm; thus, his family members did not dare to enshroud him. Later, he returned to life and recounted: "When I first died, someone led me to the presence of King Yama.
The King asked, 'Throughout your entire life, what meritorious deeds have you performed? Wenchang replied, 'My family is poor and has no—"
"One may cultivate merit through effort; one need only focus the mind on reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Upon hearing these words, the King joined his palms, bowed his head, and praised him, saying, "Excellent! Since you uphold the *Prajñā*, your merit is truly vast.
The King then dispatched attendants to lead Wang Chang toward the scripture repository to retrieve the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Wang Chang traveled westward for five or six li.
He saw several dozen rooms that were exceedingly magnificent, filled everywhere with scriptures. Their golden rollers and precious cases were exquisitely adorned.
Wenchang joined his palms and closed his eyes; he drew out a scroll at random. Upon opening it, he found it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Wenchang carried it to the King’s presence and had one person hold the scroll on the west side, while Wenchang stood on the east, facing [the King].

He recited the scripture without missing a single character. The King was greatly delighted and immediately released Chang to return home. He ordered Wen Chang to be led out through the southern gate;
at the entrance, he saw Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou in a side room by the gate, wearing three layers of shackles and chains, who called out to Chang, saying, "You are a native of my own country.
You have come here for a short time, and I wish to speak with you. Wen Chang [responded].
He immediately prostrated himself before him. The Emperor asked, "Do you recognize me? Wen Chang replied, "Your servant formerly served as a guard to Your Majesty.
Emperor Wu said, "Since you were my former minister, now that you have returned home, go to the Emperor of Sui on my behalf and recount all my crimes.
I wish for them all to be settled; however, only the crime of destroying the Buddha-dharma is so grave that it cannot be avoided. I hope you will perform a small service for me in this regard."
"By virtue of this merit, I hope that through these blessings I may be freed from hell. Chang accepted his words and departed.
Upon reaching the southern gate, he saw a large pit of excrement with a person's hair protruding from it.

Chang questioned the man leading him there, who replied, "This is Bai Qi, the General of Qin, who is confined here; his offenses are not yet exhausted. Chang returned home and was restored to life. Thereupon, he...

He reported this matter to the Emperor. The Emperor ordered that a tax on grain exports be levied throughout the realm to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the sake of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou.
A great offering was established for three days, and the proceedings were subsequently recorded and included in the history of the Sui dynasty (*Taiping Guangji*).

Kang Cheng examined the records of this netherworld office; they contained only the names of people and lacked virtually any other details.

The official said, "These are all those who will die by the blade in the coming year. Kang Cheng asked, "Is there one among them that is me? If so, please check and show it to me. The official replied, "There is."
He was greatly startled and said, "Since you were formerly my official, could you not have some feeling for me? He replied, "That is precisely why I have come to inform the Illustrious Lord.
Only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* can be entrusted; I shall lose my life for it. Thereupon, he proceeded to read the *Vajracchedikā*, several dozen times each day.
The following year, Zhu Ci indeed rebelled. He appointed [Kang Cheng] as a Censor, but Kang Cheng rebuked Ci, saying, "You rebel subject dares to interfere with a man of state!"

Li Ci was struck with rage and ordered several hundred cavalrymen to surround him and shoot at him. Kang Cheng silently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and not a single arrow caused him harm.
Li Ci said, "The Confucians take loyalty and good faith as their armor; this is indeed true. He then desisted and departed.
Kang Cheng subsequently retired to live in seclusion on Mount Zhongnan and never again entered government service (from the *Baoying ji*).
Xue Yan of the Tang dynasty served as the Sima of Zhongzhou. He maintained a vegetarian diet and observed the perpetual fast, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā Sūtra* thirty times every day.
When he reached the age of seventy-two and was about to pass away, he saw banners, canopies, and music coming to welcome him. His wife, Lady Cui, was the daughter of the Censor An...
Yan’s paternal aunt was lying on her deathbed when she saw Yan following behind banners and canopies as they ascended slowly toward heaven.
She called out to him, but he did not look back. The entire family perceived the fragrance of a wondrous incense (from the *Baoying ji*).
Ren Zixin, Ren Zixin, was a native of Jiazhou. In the fifteenth year of the Zhengyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he traveled to Hunan.

He constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which remained pure and white without a single blemish. While on Lake Dongting, a strange object like a cloud suddenly enveloped his boat; in an instant—

The boat dispersed, and the monks within lost their confidence, not knowing where they were. After a long time, they emerged upon the waves and said that they had reached the Dragon Palace to pay their respects to the Dragon King.
Four or five people ordered them to ascend the hall to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, after which they were given dozens of precious jewels and pearls.
Two monks escorted them out of the palace; one monk entrusted a small amount of these gifts to a believer to deliver to Mount Heng at the Guanyin Terrace.
He transmitted it to Master Shaozhen, saying, "Your preceptor sent this to you; have him recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
[Shaoshen] then went to Mount Nanyue to visit a monk and indeed saw him. The monk said, "The Preceptor passed away five or six years ago" (*Baoying ji*).
Duan Wenchang was in the seventeenth year of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty. Duan Wenchang traveled from Qi to Shu to respond to the summons of Wei Gao, the Prince of Nan’gang.
When Wei reached his later years, he was slandered by a favorite of the enemy; consequently, Duan was appointed as Acting Magistrate of Lingchi County. Wei soon passed away.

When Li Wenchang learned that Cao Pi had been appointed as the Acting Governor (liuhou), he recalled that he and Pi had long been at odds. Upon hearing the news, he left the county overnight and reached the eastern gate of the city.
Shortly thereafter, Pi issued a decree forbidding officials from various counties from leaving their posts. That evening, a dark wind began to blow as Wenchang was returning.

Having traveled two *li* outside the city walls, he saw two torches flanking the road for a hundred paces, serving as a guide. At first, he thought it was the county officials coming out to welcome him; however, finding this strange...
It was neither early nor late; whether high or low, far or near, there was not the slightest discrepancy. When it reached the outskirts of the county seat, the light began to fade;

by the time it reached the gate, the county officials had still not yet received the official notice from the prefecture. At that time, Wenchang had been reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for five or six years, never missing a single day.

It is indeed true that supreme sincerity must evoke a response, and where there is a response, there must be a sign. The aforementioned Daoist practitioners on the left and right were those who had left traces recorded in the scriptures.

Later, as his rebellious conduct gradually became manifest, the Emperor appointed Yuan Zizi as the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi). Wenchang’s younger cousin, having served in the military since his youth, was in charge of affairs at the Left Camp;
fearing he would be implicated in the calamity, he conspired with the Military Commissioner to communicate by means of wax-sealed pellets and silk letters.
He plotted with Yuan, but the matter soon came to light, and he was entirely devoured by the rebels. At that time, Wenchang was aware of the plot;
as he recited sutras late into the night, he did not notice himself falling into a weary sleep. With all the doors and gates closed, he suddenly heard someone open the door and enter.
He spoke of his fearlessness more than twice. When an object was thrown against the door, it made a sudden, loud noise; as he started up in alarm, the sound was still ringing in his ears.
He looked to his left and right, but both the officials and the servants were fast asleep. He ordered torches to be lit and searched everywhere, yet at first nothing was seen.
However, the door that had been closed moments before was now wide open. Wen Chang had recited this sutra over one hundred thousand times, and the response was manifest.
[Recorded in] *Chuyanglizhu*. Liu Yihuai of the Tang dynasty was in Bianzhou at that time.
Han Hong served as the Right Wing Commander, while the Marquis of Yu, Wang [Surname], served as the Left Wing Commander. Yu...
Hou and Hong were on good terms. Some suggested that the two men were harboring ulterior military intentions and would not act in Liu’s best interest.

Liu was greatly incensed and summoned both to interrogate them. Hong was Liu’s nephew; he pressed his forehead to the ground and spoke with great resolve, whereupon Liu’s suspicions were somewhat dispelled.
Mr. Wang was advanced in years; his thighs trembled so that he could not even distinguish himself. Liu the Commander dragged him to sit down and struck him thirty times with a staff.

At that time, new red clubs had been made, their heads several inches in diameter and reinforced with sinew and lacquer; when stood upright, they would not fall over. Wang was likely to die after five or six blows.
Han thought he must surely be dead, yet when he visited his house at dusk, he found it strange that there were no sounds of wailing, and further remarked that [Wang] must not dare [to speak].
He wept. Upon inquiring at the gate of the military post, the guards said, "The Great Envoy is unharmed. As Senghong was well-acquainted with him, he went directly to his quarters to question him.

[Senghong] said, "I have been reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for forty years, yet it was only now that I truly gained its power. I remember the moment I first sat down [to recite it]."
He saw a giant hand, as large as a winnowing basket, suddenly appear and shield his back. He then bared his shoulder to show it to Han; there were no marks from the lash at all.

Previously, Han had not been fond of the Śākya teachings, but because of this, he began to associate with the monks. Every day he would transcribe ten sheets himself, and by the time he attained high office, the count reached several hundred fascicles.
Later, while serving in the Chancellery during the height of summer, an official of remonstrance came to visit him on business; Han was in the midst of writing while covered in sweat.
The monk admonished him for his strange inquiry and asked why he had questioned him so. Han then related in detail the matter concerning Wang (from the *Yinhualu*).
During the time when Sun Xian was serving under Liang Chongyi in Xiangzhou before the rebellion broke out, a minor general named Sun Xian died suddenly; after two nights and one day...
Upon reviving, he said that he had arrived at a place like the residence of a king, where the ceremonial guards were extremely strict.

An official led a monk before him for questioning; the monk’s dharma name was Huaixiu. He had been dead for over a year, and during his life he had severely violated the precepts. Upon entering the underworld, it was found that there were no good deeds to record.
He then falsely claimed, "I always instructed my grandson Xian to copy the Lotus Sutra. The official then commanded Xian to be summoned for interrogation.
At first, both brothers did not acknowledge their guilt. The monk insisted upon it, and after some time had passed without a resolution, they suddenly saw a śramaṇa who said, "Dizang has spoken thus:
'If you disciples confess, you will also receive protection yourselves. They then followed these words and consequently escaped harm.

He further recounted that during the interrogation, he saw a King of the Rong people arrive from outside with several hundred guards; the Lord of the Netherworld descended the steps and met him level with his own.
He ascended the hall and sat down. Not long after, a great wind swept him away. He then saw another person being interrogated regarding their merits and transgressions.

This man had regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, yet he also enjoyed eating meat. To his left were several thousand fascicles of the sutra; to his right, piles of meat formed a mountain.
Because of the abundance of meat, he was about to be brought in for severe judgment. Suddenly, from within the heap of sutras, a spark of fire flew forth.
The mountain of flesh vanished in an instant. The man then ascended into the air and departed. Xian asked Dizang, "Where did the wind from the foreign king blow him to?
Dizang replied, "That king shall enter the Avīci Hell; the wind you felt was the wind of karma. He then led Xian to view the hells.
Upon reaching the gate, smoke and flames blazed fiercely, and the sound was like wind and thunder. They were struck with fear.
He did not dare to look. Upon looking down at the cauldron of boiling water, droplets of splashing foam fell upon his left thigh, causing a pain that pierced to his very marrow.

Kṣitigarbha ordered an official to escort him back, forbidding him from leaking any matters of the underworld. When he returned, it was as if he were dreaming; his wife and children had been weeping around him for a full day.

He subsequently depleted his household wealth to copy the scriptures and requested to leave the secular life. The spot where the droplets had fallen in his dream became a sore that remained for the rest of his life.
[From the *Youyang zazu*]. Monk Zhideng:
During the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Zhideng at Tianchong Temple in Jingzhou who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He fell ill and died.
The disciple reported that his hands were still warm and had not yet been placed in the coffin. After seven days, he returned to life. Initially, he saw a king-like figure in the underworld;
because he had recited the sutras, the figure joined his palms and descended from the steps. He then inquired, saying, "I grant you, Venerable Sir, ten more years in this world;
strive to transcend birth and death. He further asked, "Among the monks in the human realm, do they eat *yǐyǐrén* (coix lacryma-jobi) and medicinal herbs after the midday meal?"
To eat this is a great violation of the fundamental teachings. *Dengbao* says: "How can there be provisions for both permission and prohibition within the Vinaya?
He replies: "This was added by later generations; it is not the Buddha’s intention. Currently, among the monastic community in Jingzhou, there are none who drink medicinal decoctions (*Yuyang zazu*).

Wang Conggui, a commoner of Chancheng Village in Gongan County during the Wang clan’s reign, had a younger sister who had not yet been married and regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

During the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, she suddenly died of a violent illness. Three days after she had been buried, her family covered the tomb when they heard the sound of groaning coming from within it. Thereupon...
He opened his eyes to see; indeed, a vapor was rising. After returning home for several days, he was able to speak. He said:
"When I first arrived in the underworld, the officials of the nether realm released me back because of my merit in upholding the scriptures.
Wang Conggui was skilled at carpentry and once constructed Linghua Temple at Gong'an. The monk Shuzhong once heard Conggui recount this story" (from *Youyang zazu*).

During the time when Wei Gao, the Prince of Nan’gang, was stationed in Shu, there was a soldier of the left guard who, while on patrol at the western mountain encampment, studied the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with his fellow fire-guard comrades.
He was by nature stubborn; on the first day, he had only just mastered the title of the scripture when that night, at the watchtower—
Outside, he gathered firewood to serve as a fence, which was bound and carried away by horsemen. After traveling more than a hundred *li*, they stopped.
Before dawn, they threw him to the ground, tied his hair to a wooden stake, and covered him with felt rugs, placing him upon them. This man thought only of the title of a sutra;
suddenly, he saw a bar of gold emitting light standing before him. He tried to lift his head and move his body, and all his bonds fell away. Thereupon, he slipped away in secret.
He rose and pursued the gold ingot, running until he had traveled some ten-odd *li*. Before dawn, he realized he had already arrived home.
His home was in the Eastern Market of the Prefecture. His wife and children initially suspected him of being a ghost, but he explained the circumstances of his journey in detail.

Five or six days after his arrival, the commander of the military camp finally reported his escape. At first Wei did not believe it, but when the day of the escape coincided exactly with the day of his arrival home, he finally [believed it].
Exemption from [the examination] (from the *Youyang zazu*). Song Kankan was a native of the Jianghuai region.
He had been prepared to take the examination for the Mingjing degree, but by the beginning of the Yuanhe era, he reached Heyin County and became incapacitated due to illness.
Ye served as a scribe for the Salt and Iron Office, receiving two thousand coins per month; he married and lived in comfort, never considering any other occupation.
After more than a year, a grain convoy passing through the Three Gates arrived. Because Ye was illiterate, he requested that Kǎn accompany him to manage the accounts.
The monthly stipend was eight thousand coins. Kǎn said to his wife, "For several months now we have not received eight thousand; if even one..."
He arrived there in the month of [the lunar calendar], which was extremely auspicious. His wife, Lady Yang, was exceptionally virtuous;

she urged him not to go, saying, "The boat route through the Three Gates is quite treacherous. Should you meet with peril, what benefit could possibly save you? Yuankan did not accept her advice and departed nonetheless.
Upon reaching his destination, he was indeed struck by a violent storm. All the other ships were submerged, but Yuankan alone reached down into the water and grasped a bale of grain straw.
A bundle of straw gradually drifted near the shore; floating upon it, he emerged and was restored to life. The remaining dozens of people were all not saved.
He then embraced the straw and thanked it, saying, "This humble life of mine is a gift from you. I swear that whether in life or death, we shall never part.
He then clutched the straw and hurried for several li until he reached a solitary old woman’s two-room thatched hut where she sold tea, and there he went to stay the night.
He reported the matter in full. The old woman took pity on him and prepared some gruel for him. When morning came, she was hanging clothes to dry in the south part of the house;
as she untied the straw bundles to sun them, she found a bamboo tube among the straw. Upon opening it, she discovered it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
She immediately informed the old man, yet neither of them knew its provenance. The old woman said, "Since you arrived, your wife has been bowing with disheveled hair."
"Because your devotion in transcribing the sutra was so sincere, I have been able to save you. Kǎn wept with gratitude and requested to return home.
The old woman pointed toward the southeast along a path and said, "Just follow this; it is two hundred li away, and you will reach home the day after tomorrow. She gave him two sheng of rice.
Having offered his thanks, he set out. Indeed, in two days he reached Heyin. Upon seeing him, [the official] apologized for his previous conduct. Lady Yang asked in surprise, "How did you know this?
He recounted the entire matter from its beginning. Lady Yang was astonished; Huan then produced the scripture, which Lady Yang wept over as she prostrated herself and placed it upon her head.
Huan asked, "What can be used as proof? She replied, "When it was being transcribed, the scribe mistakenly wrote the character for 'Arhat' (luóhàn) instead of 'Ratna' (línà)."
