The Master was elderly and his vision was failing, so his brushstrokes were too heavy and the characters were all dark and blurred. However, for ten days he had not known where they were. Upon inspection, it was indeed as he had said.
Kuan wept even more bitterly and bowed to the Master’s wife. Every day he burned incense and paid homage to the scriptures in a pure place.
In her chamber, she said to Lady Yang, "I must not forget the old woman by the riverbank. She dispatched a messenger with tea and silk to give to her.
When the messenger arrived, neither the dwelling nor the person were to be seen. He questioned the cowherds, who replied, "Recently the waters have risen without limit;
how could there be anyone selling tea? They further stated that the path was likewise non-existent. This was clearly a divine manifestation. It continued for several years.
When Zheng Gongyin was the Imperial Commissioner for the Eastern Capital, he summoned Kan and Yang Yuan to inquire about the origins of the scripture and ordered them to bring it forth.
He provided them with official provisions and a monthly stipend of five thousand coins. Subsequently, he sought out the scripture, which has been venerated by the Zheng family to this day.
Thus, when the Prime Minister, the Duke of Hongnong—who had served as the Prefect of Yuezhou—beheld it...
The matter was subsequently recorded; it is titled "The Miraculous Verification of Lady Yang" (from the *Baoying ji*).
In the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, an imperial edict was issued stating that all small Buddhist halls in villages throughout the empire were to be demolished.
The imperial decree was transferred to a nearby Buddhist temple. All large halls were ordered to be sealed off.
Heretics throughout the empire, upon hearing the wind of this command, began tearing them down; even great buildings and colossal Buddha statues were destroyed.

When the edict reached Yuzhou, Li Xu, the Magistrate of Xinxi, was a man who indulged in wine and was arrogant and perverse in his conduct. He was still intoxicated when the provincial summons arrived, with a three-day deadline imposed.

Xujian was greatly incensed and immediately issued a decree that anyone within the jurisdiction who tore down [the buildings] would be put to death. Consequently, the entire precinct was preserved intact.
Xujian was by nature fond of killing and obstinately cruel; his actions invariably contravened the Way. At that time, it was not out of any regard for the Buddhist temple that he acted thus.

He preserved his integrity solely because of his resentment and indignation; yet even while maintaining this integrity, he did not dwell upon it. After more than a year, he died from a chronic illness after several days.

It was the height of summer, and ten days later his body was encoffined. The following day, as they were about to prepare for the burial, the mother and son circumambulated the coffin and wailed for him.

After a long night, the weeping ceased. From within the coffin, there was heard a sound like fingernails scratching against the wood; at first he suspected it was a rat, but he did not realize what it was.

In an instant, the pain intensified greatly. His wife and children fled in alarm, but his mother alone did not leave. She ordered the coffin opened. Those around her said, "It is the height of summer;
we fear it will spoil. The mother grew angry and urged them to open it. Inside was someone who had been born prematurely. His body was somewhat ulcerated and decayed.

Thereupon, she bathed him and nursed him back to health. After more than a month, he recovered. Xu said, "At first, I was seized by two soldiers and brought before the King. The King did not look at me; he looked [at something else]."
The clerk standing before the steps was actually an official from Xinxi who had been dead for years. Seeing Xu, he bowed and asked, "How have you managed to come here, Official?
Xu replied, "I have just been summoned and arrived. The clerk said, "Throughout your life, you were solely intent on killing and harming;
you knew nothing of sin or merit. Now you must undergo retribution—what will you do? Hearing this, Xu was terrified and begged for his rescue.
The official said, "Last year, when the Buddha hall was demolished, yours was the only one within the jurisdiction of the magistrate to remain intact.
This merit is immense; even though the magistrate is dead, it is not appropriate for him to be summoned here. Before long, the King will question you, so do not say anything more.
Simply answer him with these words. [When he] forgets, remind him. Shortly thereafter, as the King sat, the master led Xu to see the King. The King said, "I seek Magistrate Li."
The register of good and evil arrived. Immediately, someone brought a set of documents as large as a man's full embrace, followed by two youths dressed in green.
The King ordered the records to be opened and the offenses proclaimed. A court official read them aloud: "He was exclusively fond of cutting off the hooves of sheep."
The official said, "He deserves one hundred strokes of the cane. He then ordered that a hundred jin of the man's flesh be cut off. The King said, "Let his flesh be cut.
Daoxu said, "Last year there was an imperial edict to dismantle Buddhist halls and destroy Buddha images. Within my jurisdiction, I alone preserved them.
Can this merit cancel out my sin? The King asked in surprise, "Is this truly so? The official replied, "It is not. An official from Xinxi stepped forward and said:
"There is. Their registers of merit are in heaven; you may inspect them. The King said, "Inspect them promptly. Ahead of the palace wall to the south, there were several rooms on a tower.
An official ascended the tower to inspect them, but before he had arrived, two monks came to the front of the hall.

The King asked, "What do you masters possess? One replied, "I constantly recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The other said, "I constantly read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King rose and joined his palms in reverence.
He said, "Please ask the Dharma Master to ascend the steps. Behind the royal throne were two high seats; the one on the right was of gold, and the one on the left was of silver.
The King requested that the reciter sit upon the golden seat and the reader sit upon the silver seat. Once they were seated, the sutra was opened. The King joined his palms and listened.
As the recitation and reading were nearing completion, suddenly five-colored clouds appeared before the golden seat, and purple clouds appeared before the silver seat. The two monks—
Riding upon the clouds, they flew away and vanished into the air. The King asked the people below the steps, "Did you see the two monks?

They have both been reborn in heaven. Thereupon, the officials brought forth the registers of good deeds; there was but a single sheet of paper. Reading it, he said: "Last year, by imperial decree, Buddhist halls were demolished. Xinxi alone preserved one life.
For this act of saving a life, his transgressions are to be expunged and his lifespan extended by thirty years; he shall furthermore be reborn in a realm of goodness."
"Way! As he finished speaking, fire burst forth from within the scrolls of the register of sins and consumed them entirely. The King said, "Release Magistrate Li and let him return.

He then commanded two officials to escort him out through the southern city gate. There, he saw high pavilions lining both sides of the road, where men and women of all ages sat in rows, drinking and singing to the accompaniment of flutes and songs.
Delighted by the empty splendor of the string and wind instruments, the two officials said to him, "Hurry past this place."
Xu Wugou thought to himself, "To look back would surely cause some harm; however, seeing this place of drink, my mind cannot bear it. He stood there for a while observing it.

A man from the tavern called out, "Come here! Xu said, "This is no good place. The man replied, "If you do not trust me, you may go as you please. Xu had not yet realized the situation, so he went to the drinking place.
Everyone rose to greet him as he took his seat. String and wind instruments were played, and wine was served. After Xu had finished the ritual of mutual salutations and pouring, he was about to—
He was told to drink it; it was a cup of excrement, foul and loathsome beyond measure.
Xu refused to drink it, whereupon a bull-headed hell-warden emerged from beneath the bed and pierced his chest with a fork. In desperation, Xu hastily drank several cups and was then released.
The officials led Xu Nan into a narrow path through a desolate field. From afar, they saw a lamp burning brightly; beside the lamp was a great pit, dark and bottomless.
The two officials pushed him into it, whereupon he regained consciousness. Li Xu was by nature fierce and stubborn, ignorant of both sin and merit;
yet, having been intoxicated, he acted with such defiance as to completely restore the Buddha hall—this was clearly not his original intention. Nevertheless...
If even one who has already been born in heaven can have their record of sins incinerated by fire and obtain such blessings, is this not the retribution for doing good?
As for those who exert themselves with diligent perseverance day and night to do good— upholding the monastic precepts and constantly practicing the Buddha’s words—
it has never happened that they have failed to transcend birth and death (from *Jiwen*).

During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a man of the Lu clan who resided in Huazhou. One day, while sitting in his courtyard during the daytime with the doors closed, he saw two men wearing yellow tunics enter the gate.
Lu asked, "Who are you? They replied, "We are the village headmen (lizheng) sent with a warrant to summon you. Lu was greatly... [frightened].
He was struck with astonishment and asked why he was being pursued. He then requested to inspect the official document (*tiē*), finding the seal impressed with the characters for "Wei County.

Upon opening it, he saw that the writing was erroneous and did not resemble the hand of a human being. Feeling strange, he interrogated the official. The official said, "I have received orders to pursue you; I do not know the reason.
Suddenly, he saw a horse already prepared at the foot of the steps. Having no choice, he mounted the horse and departed, looking back as he went.
The corpse sat upon the bed; his heart felt profound revulsion toward it, yet in the midst of such urgency, he did not realize it was dead.
Furthermore, he saw horses emerging not through the gates but all traveling along the walls; he was struck with such terror that he could not weep, only then realizing he must die.

Regretting that he could not take leave of his mother and sisters, he traveled for several tens of *li* until he reached a city. The city was most magnificent and grand. He asked, "What is this place?"
The city official said, "This is indeed King Shi's market. He immediately sent for the official in charge of the guest. After entering the city, the official wished to present Lu to the king.
As they passed by a courtyard, he asked, "What courtyard is this? The official replied, "This is the courtyard of the Grand Master of Censorship.

He then asked the name and surname of the Grand Master. [The official] said, "His surname is Li and his given name is So-and-so. Lu was filled with joy and surprise, and said to the official, "This is my cousin. He then ordered—
The official conveyed his message, and shortly thereafter he came out. They met with great joy and spoke at length of their past acquaintances.
He invited him in to sit and converse. The Grand Master said, "Your younger brother’s merit from recitation is truly vast;

this is because the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāra-mitā Sūtra* is the very marrow of the holy teachings, possessing profound and inconceivable merit. When Lu first entered the monastery, he saw several dozen...
The people there were all dressed in official robes and caps. Later, more than half of them became entangled in nets; some were without clothing, while others had their heads bared.
Lu asked, "Who are all these people? They replied, "These are officials from the land of Yangdi. Those within the nets are all here because their offenses are grave.
If you, my brother, could preach the Dharma for them once, all who see it would attain rebirth in heaven. He then ordered a high seat to be brought and had Lu ascend it.
As they recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, those within the net began to show their heads; by the midpoint of the recitation, they had all emerged upon the ground.
Some wore wide-sleeved robes of fine silk, while others rode in carriages or drove through the clouds. When the recitation was finished, everyone had been reborn.
Upon entering for an audience, the King addressed them as "Dharma Masters" and paid them profound respect. The King said, "You have done a great thing..."
It was inconceivable; even calculation could not reach its limit. He marveled at the power of her recitation and immediately ordered the official to send her back.

Upon arriving home, he saw her family members with disheveled hair, weeping, while her corpse lay upon the floor. His heart was deeply moved by compassion. Suddenly, a maidservant entered the hall from the courtyard;
the official ordered her to follow [the woman] up the stairs and forward, whereupon her spirit suddenly re-entered her body. Because of this—
This man was subsequently revived (from the *Guang yiji*).
As for Wang Hong:
in his youth, he made his living as a hunter and fisherman. During the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, he once released a hawk to pursue a hare and fled.
Xue Hong followed and explored it, whereupon he obtained one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. From that time on, he ceased hunting altogether (from the *Guang yi ji*).
*Biographies of the Miraculous Efficacy of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
*Biographies of Miraculous Responses to the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Middle Volume.
Zhang Jiayou of Guangling was the Sima of Mingzhou during the early Baoying era of the Tang dynasty. He fell ill and passed away; his funeral procession was then carrying the coffin.

He returned home and was buried outside the South Gate of Guangling. At the beginning of the Yongtai era, one of his former acquaintances named Lao was traveling south of the city wall when he sat down beneath a stupa.
Suddenly, he saw Sengyou riding a white horse coming from the south. Lao dismounted and greeted him as they had done in life;
however, You did not remove his official cap and spoke with his head bowed. Lao asked, "Is there [a world] within the darkness?"
"What are sin and merit? Yu replied, "Sin and merit are manifest; there is nothing that is not obtained in accordance with what one does.

However, I have long maintained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and now I have attained freedom from karmic entanglement. I shall also depart for another destination within the span of a month or two.
When you return, convey this to my elder brother and have him recite the *Vajracchedikā* one thousand times. Why would you take my incense burner and fill it..."
"Those wicked things! Your family also possesses two fascicles of scripture; I would be grateful if you would recite them for me to increase my own merit.
Having said this, he took his leave and departed. [The narrator] was so exhausted and dazed that it took a long time before he finally regained consciousness (from the *Guang yi ji*).

Chen Zhao of the early Yuanhe period: Chen Zhao, a clerk in the administrative office of Hanzhou, was once ill when he saw a man dressed in yellow clothes approach his bedside and say, "Judge Zhao summons you.
Zhao asked for the reason; the man replied, "I have come from the underworld. Liu Pi..."
He was engaged in legal proceedings with the district magistrate of Dou, who had summoned him to serve as a witness. Zhao immediately sat down and waited for a while.

Another man appeared, holding an object like a fetal membrane. The official in charge marveled at his tardiness, to which he replied, "It is precisely because I am waiting for the butcher's shop to open.
He then said to Zhao with a smile, "Do not be afraid. To take the breath of a living person, one must obtain a pig’s bladder. You may stand to the side facing east."
As he lay down, Zhao followed his words; before he knew it, he had been led by two officials along a very level road for over ten *li*.
They arrived at a city as large as a provincial capital, where armored soldiers guarded the gates. Upon entering, he saw a man with a terrifyingly wrathful countenance—it was Officer Zhao.
He said, "Liu Pi has been defeated in Dongchuan, and Douxian has seized forty-seven head of cattle to send [to him]."
In Zizhou, it was reported that Liu Pi had issued a warrant for execution. Pi further stated, "Previously there was no official document;
you, as the clerk in charge of records, ought to know the facts of the matter. Before he could respond, he heard from across the wall the voice of Du calling out, "Where is Chen Zhao?

When asked about the survival of his brothers, wife, and children, Zhao immediately wished to have an audience with him. The underworld official said, "The appearance of Lord Du is extremely hideous; [do not approach him]."
He wished to see him. The official then explained in detail that the actual reason for killing the ox was to serve Liu Shangshu, and that it was not for the sake of the official document.
The paper was made of hemp and was currently on a private shelf in a certain room in Hanzhou. He immediately ordered the official to lead Zhao to Hanzhou to retrieve it.
Since the gates and halls were locked, he entered and exited through a small opening in the wall. When he arrived and delivered the details, [Liu] opened the door and remained silent. Zhao...
Zhao said, "Zhaor, you have committed a transgression yourself; do you know it? As for the ox slaughtered at Xian County, you took one of its heads.
Before Zhaor could reply, Zhao said, "This is not like the human world; nothing can be feigned. In a moment, a soldier will arrive dragging the ox head.

Zhaor was immediately struck with fear and begged for mercy. Zhao ordered that the legal statutes be consulted, and it was determined that he deserved one hundred blows of the cane and five years of penal servitude.
On the tenth day, Zhao said to Zhaozao, "What meritorious deeds do you possess? Zhao immediately recounted that she had once hosted several vegetarian feasts and painted Buddhist images.
Zhao [of Shu] said, "These will bring you blessings in a future life. Zhaozao further stated that she had once read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at her cousin's house.
Zhao said, "Then you should join your palms and request it. Zhaozao did as she was told. After a short while, she saw the sutra, wrapped in a yellow cloth, descend from the sky.
Then he descended and stayed before Zhao. Zhao took it and looked at it; it was the very copy his elder cousin had borrowed. The burn marks on the binding were still visible.
Again he joined his palms in reverence, and the scripture immediately vanished. Zhao said, "This is sufficient to spare me," and he released him.
He then ordered Zhao to go to an office called Shenglu (Office of Life and Fortune) to have his lifespan examined. The official reported: "Zhao’s original name is Jiao. He is a man of gold."
Pángdāo. In that year, it was changed to Zhāo. He lived for another eighteen years. When Zhāo heard this, he was filled with sorrow.

Zhào laughed and said, "In these eighteen years, have you not had much cause for joy? Are you unhappy? He then ordered an official to escort Zhāo back. On the way, they encountered a horse blocking the road.
The official said, "This is your original property; you may ride it. Zhāo immediately mounted it and was restored to life. He had been dead for half [a day].
Recorded in the *Youyang zazu*. In the third year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, Wang Zhonggan was appointed.
Li Tongjie obstructed the army at Cangzhou; Emperor Jing ordered Li You to command the Qi-de [Army].

The army went to suppress them. Initially, they surrounded the city of Dezhou; though the city was strong, it could not be taken. On the following day, they attacked it again from the hour of Māu (5 a.m.
until Wèi (1–3 p.m.). Nearly eighteen or nineteen percent of the troops were wounded, yet in the end, they still could not take it.

At that time, there was an officer of the eight generals in the headquarters of Qizhou named Jiǎnróng, a man of Zhōnggàn in Bóyě County, who had long been devoted to reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for over twenty years, never missing a single day.
On that day, Zhonggan ascended the flying ladder; as he was about to reach the battlements, his body was pierced by arrows like a porcupine.

He was brought down by a *lei-mu* (a heavy wooden beam) and dragged out of the Yangma City by his fellow fire-soldiers. They placed him on the bank of the moat at dusk and ordered the withdrawal of the troops.
At that time, arrows fell from the city walls like rain. His comrades were so frantic that they forgot to retrieve Zhonggan’s corpse. Zhonggan—

Having died, he was as if in a dream. Arriving at a wilderness, he encountered a great river; wishing to cross it, he found no means to do so and wept aloud toward the heavens. Suddenly, he heard the sound of human voices.
Zhonggan saw a man over ten feet tall and, suspecting him to be a divine being, requested that he be shown the way to the camp.
The man said, "Do not be afraid. I shall enable you to cross this river. Zhonggan bowed to him; as soon as his head lowered—

Before he could lift himself up, a divine being seized him by the waist and threw him into the air; it was only after a long time that he landed on the ground. Suddenly, as if awakening from a dream, he heard the second watch being struck atop the city wall of the rebels.

At first, he did not remember crossing the water, nor was he aware of his wound. When he raised his hand to feel his face, he found blood smeared upon his eyebrows and eyelashes, and only then realized he had been injured.
He then tried to walk forward with all his strength for over a hundred paces, but then collapsed again, whereupon he saw the man who had previously assisted him.
Brandishing his blade, he shouted, "Arise! Arise! Zhonggan was struck with terror and fled for over a li before sitting down to rest.
It was only then that he heard the shouts of his own army; upon reaching his camp, he sought out his fellow soldiers and learned that his body lay dead on the bank of the moat.
This was the river he had crossed in his dream (from the *Youyang zazu*).
Wang Cheng, whose family resided in Jinyang, was by nature stubborn and base. In the fourth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, a plague broke out in his household and many died.
When he was eighteen or nineteen, he was suddenly stricken with illness. He ate dog meat, whereupon his eyes became blind.

Not knowing of medical treatment, he prayed only to ghosts and spirits, yet for several years there was no response. Suddenly, a strange monk came to request alms and said to him, "In the scriptures of our Master there is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
It can dispel all sufferings, and its karmic retribution is swift and miraculous. Layman, would you be able to receive it? Daoci declined.

Being foolish and moreover blind, he was certainly unable to memorize it. The monk urged him to transcribe it, and Cheng followed his advice. He obtained seven fascicles and invited the monk to stay for several days.
One night, he dreamed that the aforementioned monk took a knife and gouged out his eyes; he then woke up in a startle. Upon awakening, he found that he could see again.
After a long time, it became completely clear; for several months, it was as it had been before. Cheng recited the sutras for the rest of his life without ceasing (*from the *Baoying ji*).
Li Yuanyi: during the fifth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, Li Yuanyi served as the Sima of Raozhou. He had a daughter living in a separate courtyard who, in the middle of the night...
Suddenly she saw a divine being; struck with terror, she died, yet her facial expression remained unchanged.
Her husband, Yan Ne, had come from Qin to Canghu when he vaguely saw his wife walking upon the water. Startled, he questioned her, and she wept, saying, "I have already passed away;
I am now a ghost. Ne was struck with awe and wonder, and said, "Nearby, at Yanshipu Village, there is a Master Yan."
He instructed the assembly to study. That man possessed extraordinary arts; the Duke went to him and earnestly entreated him for compassionate rescue, saying, "I hope that I may yet return to life.

Later, Nyeong-nal indeed met Master Yeom. He prostrated himself and wept as he recounted his story, disclosing the entire root of the matter. At first, Master Yeom was extremely angry, saying, "The young master suffers from a wind-illness;
why has he been so mistreated? Nyeong-nal bowed again and wept bitterly for a long time. Only then did the Master grant permission, saying, "As for the one who killed the lady..."
The King was a general. He is buried beneath the northwest pillar inside this hall.

You should have the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* transcribed and have a monk recite it at his shrine. The young lady will surely return. Nae bowed in thanks and hastened to the prefectural city.
Arriving the following day, he informed Yuan-yi in full detail and urged him to transcribe the scripture and have it recited seven times immediately. Thereupon, the woman opened [the door].
After a long time, she was able to speak. She apologized to her husband, saying, "Beneath the pillar of this hall lies the withered bones of General Wang, who carries a short sword.
Please reinter him; as for the sword, I request that you keep it to repay your virtue.
When they excavated it, it was indeed so. They subsequently reburied him and kept the sword. Yuan-yi then transcribed several hundred scrolls of sutras to bestow upon the netherworld. (From...)
*Baoying ji* (Records of Retribution).
Regarding Yu Wan Ying:
In the seventh year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, there was a coarse and violent man living in the marketplace of Jingzhao whose residence was located at... [text fragment].
There was a great venomous snake; all those who saw it in the house were struck with terror. Wan Ying became enraged and, one day, waiting for it to emerge, struck and killed it with a massive club.
He then boiled and roasted its flesh to eat. Consequently, he fell ill, suffering excruciating pain in his internal organs, and eventually died.

His heart remained slightly warm, and after seven days he revived, saying: "At first, I saw three or four messengers from the underworld pursuing me away. We traveled through the darkness for ten [li]..."
In another village, he saw a man walking alone, his radiance encircling his body and illuminating for several feet on all sides as he recited a sutra from his mouth.

Wang Ying followed the light and approached him, asking for his surname and name. The man replied, "My surname is Zhao and my given name is [blank]. I am one who constantly recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
You need only not leave me. The messenger did not dare proceed further; gradually, the man vanished. After a long time, they reached his home, where Wang Ying prostrated himself.

Xie said, "Had I not encountered a supreme person, I certainly would not have returned. That man bestowed upon him the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which he was able to recite and then return home.
Upon his rebirth, he held the original text and recited it again without any omission. His illness also vanished;
consequently, he renounced wine and meat and ceased all killing. He recited the sūtra fifty times every day (*from the Baoying ji*).
Li Hui, Li Hui.

He was a candidate for the jinshi examination. In the eighth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, having failed the exam and about to return home, a monk advised him, saying, "If you, young master, wish to attain the degree quickly, why not recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? Thereupon, he recited it several dozen times every day until he reached Wangqiao.

That night, while walking under the moonlight, he encountered a beautiful woman who spoke with him. He was subsequently lured away for over ten *li* until they reached a village house where laughter and merriment were very loud.
She led him inside and up into the hall, where he saw five or six people, all of whom were young women.

Li Hui suspected they were malevolent spirits (*piśāca*), so he secretly recited a scripture. Suddenly, a strange light issued from his mouth, causing the group of women to tremble with terror and flee. However—
He smelled a rank and foul odor; it was clearly the dwelling place of foxes and badgers, with brambles and thorns filling his sight. Li Hui stood bewildered, not knowing where to go.
Suddenly, a white dog appeared, its color whiter than frost or snow, seemingly leading Li Hui forward, with light emanating from its mouth.
He again illuminated the path and, after hesitating for a moment, reached his original destination. Later, he recited it tens of thousands of times (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Qiang Boda was a native of Tang;
he lived in Fangzhou during the ninth year of the Yuanhe era. His family had suffered from a malignant disease for generations, and his descendants were afflicted from childhood.

He had suffered from the disease of wind-leprosy for two hundred years. As soon as Bo-da reached the age of twenty, he fell ill; he entrusted himself to his father and elder brothers, saying, "My illness will surely not end.
Fearing future complications, he requested to be sent into the mountains. His father and elder brothers packed provisions and escorted him to the base of a cliff.

He departed weeping and wailing. Before long, he ceased eating. Suddenly, a monk passed by and took pity on him, saying, "You should recite a four-line verse from within the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*;
perhaps you may be released from this suffering. Once Bo-da had begun the recitation, he did not cease for several days. It was then, during the day, that—
A tiger came. Fearing greatly, Bo-da simply closed his eyes and recited the gāthā with utmost sincerity. The tiger then licked his wounds all over;

he felt only a coolness as if medicinal ointment had been applied, and experienced no other suffering at all. After a long while, he looked at himself and found that the wounds were entirely healed and closed.
The next morning, the monk returned. Bo-da recounted everything in detail, whereupon the monk immediately gathered some green grass from the side of the mountain.
He grasped [the substance] and handed it to her, saying, "This can wash away the sores. Simply return home, boil this, and bathe with it.
She then wept and bowed in thanks. The monk patted her back and departed. Upon arriving home, her parents were greatly astonished; she then related the entire account from beginning to end.
After bathing, her body was bright white and entirely free of sores. From then on, the hereditary disease ceased. She recited gāthās for the rest of her life. (From...)
*Baoying ji* (Records of Retribution).
Seng Weigong,
a monk of Faxing Temple in Jingzhou during the Tang dynasty, recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* fifty times daily for over thirty years.
He was pervasive in his misconduct, disregarding monastic decorum, fond of wine, and prone to causing strife; he was loathed by the assembly of monks.
When he fell ill and was on the verge of death, there was a monk named Lingkui in the same monastery whose behavior was similar to that of Weigong; together they were a "double plague" to the temple.

On one occasion, Lingkui went out for some reason and, about one *li* from the monastery, encountered five or six men who were exceptionally handsome. Their clothing was fresh and clean, and each held a musical instrument, appearing like those from Kucha.
The Master Bu asked Lingkui, "Where is the Venerable Weigong? Lingkui immediately told him the location. Bu suspected that there was an offering being made at the temple.
When he returned to the temple later that evening, he heard the sound of bells; Weigong had already passed away. He then recounted what he had seen earlier.
On that day, the entire temple heard the sounds of stringed and wind instruments, yet no musicians entered the temple. A renowned monk of the time remarked: [This concludes the passage.]
Weiyong, having received the power of the sutra, was reborn in the Land of Immovability; he also used this account to encourage Lingkui.
Lingkui was moved to realization and humbled himself before the monastic community (from the Youyang Zazhu).

During the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, when Minister of Works Yan Souchou was stationed at Jiangling, Wang Mian, the Garrison Commander of Cenyang, regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Once, while returning from a mission to investigate affairs in Guizhou, his boat was wrecked at Zhatan. Five people were drowned together; Wang Mian— [...was among them.]
When he first entered the water, someone handed him a bamboo pole; following the waves, he emerged and submerged until he reached Xiaolao Town, where he reached the shore unharmed.
Looking at the object in his hand, it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
From Tazhan to Xiaolao Town is over three hundred li (from the *Youyang zazu*).
The Censor Zhang [surname unknown] served as an assistant censor during the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty.

While on an official mission to investigate affairs in Huainan, he was about to cross the Huai River when a man in a yellow tunic came running from behind to board the boat, claiming there was an urgent matter. Upon reaching the vessel, it was found that...
He said, "I am merely being carried across the Huai River as a passenger. The boatman wished to strike him and also reproached him, asking why he had delayed when intending to cross.
The official [the Master] said, "Do not strike him. He instead rebuked the boatman, saying, "What hardship is it to carry a single commoner across the river?
He personally fed him with leftover food. The man felt deeply ashamed. Once they had crossed, he gave [something] to the official.
They took separate paths. In a short while, they arrived at the previous station and were already at the gate. The man thought this was an invitation to plead with him;
he felt quite displeased and said, "I have just ferried you across; why have you come back again? You may leave immediately. The spirit replied, "I am truly not a human being.

I wish to discuss certain matters with the Magistrate, which are not for your subordinates to hear. He then dismissed those nearby and said, "By imperial decree, I am here to take you. It was fitting...
He drowned in the Huai River. He had just received a single meal [from the deceased], yet he remained mindful that he had received the deceased's profound kindness;
he could only stay for a single day. He requested to return to his home to leave some final instructions. The ghost said, "Beyond one day, I dare not disobey.
Although I am a messenger, my office here below is like that of a village headman or a local official in the human world. He wished—

The deceased previously requested rescue. The ghost said, "The paths of humans and ghosts are different; it is not fitting for us to press one another. I fear you cannot escape. [The deceased] offered a prostration from afar.
The ghost said, "If you can recite a thousand scrolls of the *Continuation of Life Sutra* (*Jùmìng jīng*) within a single day, your life shall be extended. Having spoken, he departed.
Upon reaching the gate, he returned and asked again, "Do you recognize the *Continuation of Life Sutra*? [The deceased] initially did not understand. The ghost said, "It is..."
"It is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The man said, "It is already late today; how could I possibly recite a thousand scrolls?
The ghost replied, "As long as a person recites it, that will suffice. The man then shouted out to those in the inn and other commoners, numbering several dozen people, to join him in the recitation.
By the following evening, they had completed the thousand repetitions. The ghost arrived again and said, "The judge has already granted you immunity."
It was necessary to visit the Underworld for a brief time. Everyone saw an official in a yellow robe accompany me as we went out the gate.

Upon seeing the King, I explained in detail that by completing one thousand recitations of the *Juxuming jing* (Sutra on Prolonging Life), my lifespan could be extended. He took up the register for inspection and found it to be exactly as I had recited.
Thereupon, I joined my palms and said, "If this is so, I should still receive ten more years of life. He then released me to be reborn. When I arrived—
At the gate, the pursuing officer said, "Because you delayed while waiting for the judgment official, you have now encountered this beating.
He then bared his chest to show it and said, "I beg for a small amount of money. The man replied, "I am but a poor scholar, and moreover, I am currently staying at an inn;

I fear it would be most inconvenient for me. The ghost said, "Only two hundred thousand. The man said, "If it were paper money, I would offer five hundred strings. The ghost said, "I am grateful for your generous intent."
"But my merit is naturally meager. By what means could I receive your promised two hundred thousand coins? The ghost said, "Now I too am but a ghost;
returning to the inn at night, it will not be easy to identify you. The ghost continued, "Official, simply think of it in your mind and have your wife and children returned;
I shall obtain them myself. The man then focused his thoughts with utmost intensity. The ghost said, "I have already received them. A short while later—

He further reported: "My wife wished to give [the money], but my grandmother was unwilling. She then instructed me to focus my mind on my grandmother; after a short while, she said, 'I have found her.

Thereupon, I became dark and unconscious, as if falling into a deep pit. Because of this, I subsequently revived. Seeking an opportunity, I returned home and related the matter in detail. My wife said it was a dream;
she had dreamed that you were already dead and that she wished to purchase [something] with two hundred thousand *qián* of paper money."
[The author] says: My grandmother once remarked, "What is there to believe in a dream?
That evening, my grandmother again had a dream, and because of it, she passed away ten years later (from the *Guang yi ji*).

Fei Ziyu was a *jianwei* (military aide) during the Tianbao era. While sleeping in his official quarters one night, he suddenly saw two officials arrive at the foot of his bed and summon him, saying, "We call for you, General Fei.
Startled, Ziyu rose and asked who they were. The officials replied, "The Great King summons you. Ziyu said:
"I am a local official; I do not belong to the kingdom of the King. Why have I been summoned? The official replied, "Yama.
Ziyu was greatly terrified and called out for someone to harness his horse, but no one responded. In desperation, he followed the official away until they reached a city.
Inside and outside the city gates, there were several thousand people each. Ziyu recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā Sūtra*, which he had habitually recited with great earnestness.
He thought to himself, "If I encounter a bodhisattva, I shall recount my grievances to him. Shortly thereafter, the King ordered him to be led inside.
Ziyu prostrated twice with great joy. Suddenly, he saw a monk descend from the clouds and pay his respects before Ziyu.
Ziyu again spoke aloud, saying, "I wish to see the Bodhisattva Dizang. The King said, "Ziyu, this is he. Ziyu stepped forward and prostrated. The Bodhisattva—
"How does Sa-yun know me? he asked. He then said to the king, "This man has recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* throughout his life;
the count of his recitations is not yet exhausted. It is fitting that you let him go. The king looked at Zi-yu and suddenly grew angry, asking for his name and surname.
Zi-yu replied, "I am Fei Zi-yu, a military aide (*canjun*) of Jiazhou. The king said, "This is Jianwei Commandery; why would you say Jiazhou? You ought—"
The Bodhisattva said, "I am currently engaged in a discourse on the suffering of death; let me first conclude this for you, my lord. Ziyu bowed twice and took his leave.
The Bodhisattva said, "Upon your return, do not eat meat again, and you shall attain eternal life. He led Ziyu to pay homage to the sacred countenance.

This sacred countenance was a bronze Buddha, whose head, face, and hands all moved. When the Bodhisattva prostrated, his hands and feet all extended. Ziyu also prostrated, and when he had finished his worship—
He went out the gate. Ziyu asked, "Why are there so many people outside the gate? The Bodhisattva said, "These people each have a lack of clarity regarding their sins and blessings;
they have been ghosts for several hundred years and have not been able to take rebirth. Ziyu took his leave and returned home, where he was revived.
Three years later, he died again while eating meat. When he was led away as a witness, the Bodhisattva saw him and became greatly enraged, saying, "I did not permit this from the beginning."
"You eat meat; why do you violate our agreement? Once Zi Yu was reborn, he consequently renounced all pungent plants and meat.
Initially, Zi Yu had taken three wives, all of whom claimed to have been summoned. They all came to see him, and Zi Yu asked how they were able to come.
His wife said, "Do not concern yourself with them. The junior wife said, "You have not been sufficient to me; I have come out of resentment. That which was used—
"Your own money—why not return it? Zi Yu replied, "Money is easy to obtain. His wife said, "He used my copper coins;
why should he now return paper money? Zi Yu said, "When a husband uses his wife's money, there is no principle by which it ought to be returned.
The wife had no reply and they parted ways after lingering for a while. (From the *Guang yiji*).
Qian Fangyi,
a Palace Attendant Censor and the son of the former Prefect of Hua Prefecture and Minister of Rites Qian Hui,

lived alone in the Changle Mansion at the beginning of the Baoli era. One night, while going to the latrine, his servant and attendants suddenly saw a man with disheveled hair and a green [complexion].
The spirit approached, its robe several feet long. Fang Yi was initially terrified and wished to flee; yet, thinking that since it was a ghost or spirit, what benefit would fleeing provide?
He then spoke forcefully to it, saying, "Are you not Guo Deng? It replied, "Yes. Fang Yi said, "Our paths are entirely different; why must we meet?
I have often heard that if people see you, they do not fail to die. Is it that my own fate was destined for death that I encountered you?"
"Yes. My younger brother Fangyi lives at home in Huazhou, and his elder sister, who is a Buddhist nun, is also here. One day she suddenly passed away.
You, sir, have commanded me with your own hand that I must not spare my regard for her; yet as a younger brother, my feelings are insufficient to allow me to face her in person and bid her farewell.
The man with the disheveled hair replied, "I am no one who harms others. My departure is also limited. Those who see me find themselves unable to withstand my righteous aura."
He has met with a violent and untimely death; it was not Deng who killed him. However, he harbored a secret intention to entrust his life to another and died while that plan remained unfulfilled.

For a long time, he did not dare to emerge. Only because your honor’s blessings and rank are boundless and your vital energy (*zhengqi*) overflows, he perceives that even if he were seen, there would be no cause for concern;
therefore, he dares to come forth to seek you. Fang Yi asked, "What do you seek? He replied, "Deng has held this office for a long time; having accumulated merit, he ought to be promoted. But..."

"Your merit is thin and you require human assistance. If a person of noble status could transcribe one scroll of the *Suvarṇavarṇa-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in golden letters and, with single-minded sincerity, offer it up for your sake, then your official position would surely advance slightly. There will certainly be a future reward;
I dare not speak falsely. Fang Yi replied, "So be it. The man with the disheveled hair spoke again: "Because Deng’s yin qi has encroached upon his yang, although the noble person possesses merit..."
His physical strength was robust and he did not suffer from illness; yet there were occasional minor ailments.

It was appropriate for him to promptly take raw rhinoceros horn and raw tortoise shell, and to plug his nostrils with musk, whereby he would have no suffering. When Fang Yi reached Zhongtang, he fainted and was on the verge of collapsing;
he immediately took musk and other medicines and plugged his nostrils, and thus had no suffering. His father’s disciple, Wang Zhifang, lived in the same village and had been there for a long time.
While engaged in affairs at the rivers and mountain passes, he sent out swift letters to procure a live rhinoceros horn, which he then consumed. After a long while, he finally recovered.

On the following morning, he selected skilled calligraphers and ordered them to transcribe three fascicles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttama-sūtra* (Golden Light Sutra) in golden characters, commanding that the work be completed early.

Once finished, he provided a meal for the monks and returned the manuscript to Guo Deng. Over a month later, he returned to his villa in Tongzhou; as soon as he dismounted and was resting, his elder brother-in-law arrived.
There was a man surnamed Pei whose family resided in E-zhu. Having been separated for ten years, he suddenly entered through the gate and went straight to the steps below Fang Yi’s residence.

Fang Yi immediately bowed to him in haste. The elder said, "I have a guest; please go out," and then proceeded forward. Fang Yi followed him, but by the time they reached the gate, he had lost sight of him.
There, he saw a man in a purple robe and an ivory tablet of office, escorted by dozens of attendants in crimson and purple garments.
A man was waiting outside the gate. When he looked down at his appearance, it was Guo Deng. Folding his ritual tablet, he stepped forward and bowed, saying, "My humble office is due for promotion;
it requires only one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Yet Your Honor, out of benevolence, has specially provided three scrolls.
Now my merit is exceedingly great, surpassing several ranks. My duties are honorable and weighty, and my rank and status are noble and eminent—all this is none other than the power of Your Honor."
Although my office has been rapidly promoted, my kitchen remains as it was before. Recently, while holding that position, I was truly like a person in a fish-market stall;

now that I have a separate office, I have come to seek food elsewhere. Only now do I realize that my former suffering was almost unbearable. May you, Noble One, examine this and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* seven times for me;
I shall change my kitchen immediately. I will engrave your virtue upon my body for the rest of my life—how could I ever dare forget it? Thus, Fang [wrote].
Yi replied, "Yes. He then asked, "Where is my elder brother? The man said, "My worthy elder brother has been ill at Tingxia for some time.
This evening his spirit was exhausted, and when he sought someone to guide him, it could not be anyone other than you. You were about to go there yourself, but he sent me back first.

He added, "The deities of the latrines customarily go on patrol every sixth day of the month. If a person encounters them on this day, disaster will surely follow; should anyone see them, [they must report it]."
He died. Anyone who saw him fell ill immediately. The former Minister of the Eight Seats had been bedridden for sixty days;

this was likely because he caught a glimpse of his half-face just as [the monk] was returning from completing a provincial tour. Among one's own relatives, each should take care to warn others and avoid him.

It is further said: "The officials of the netherworld are mostly those of meager merit. Having nothing to eat, they are constantly suffering from hunger. One must certainly share one's food with them. [He would] distribute it...
I have sacrificed to all the spirits and deities, and this mind has never forgotten them. They have all appeared before me, exerting their strength in the darkness;

they will surely rescue one from calamity and distress. Fang Yi said: "The paths of obscurity and brightness differ, yet we have happened to meet by chance. Every time I behold them, for several days my mind remains unsettled."
He expressed his intention as follows: "I would be grateful for your favor in reciting the sutras during my dreams; may the break of dawn be our appointed time. With repeated assent, he departed.
At dawn, he summoned the monk Haeng-gyeong to recite the *Diamond Sūtra* forty-nine times. When the morning came, he completed the ritual of offering prayers and entrusted them to Kŏk Dŏng-gong.
The dreamer said: "Originally I requested [the recitation] for one week, but it was extended by another six days. In total, I have received the essential food of heaven."
"Prepare the kitchen! If a noble person falls into difficulty, you must first report it to me; otherwise, do not come to trouble me with such matters.
As for requests for general sacrifices, do not forget to record them. (From the *Xu xuanguai lu*).
Banan-zai, Banan-zai.

Of the Wei clan, she constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. During the Guanghua era of the Tang dynasty, she arrived at Nixi and encountered a woman dressed in vermilion robes leading two children along with her.
They traveled together up a mountain ridge. Travelers halted and called out in a clamor as they saw them.
This was the mother of three cubs of the red-fox tiger. After hesitating for a moment, she took a different path and departed;
Wei never realized it had happened. This was due to the power of upholding the sutra (from the *Shuyiji*).
Yuanchu was a man of Yuanchu during the Yuan dynasty. A native of Jiuyang, he sold firewood in the marketplace. At the age of seventy, he constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā Sūtra*.

One evening, as he was returning from Jiangnan to Jiangbei, a great storm of wind and waves arose in midstream. While all those traveling with him perished, Yuanchu alone floated upon the water. Immediately...

He drifted to the southern bank. All those whose boats were moored there were disciples of Daci (Great Beginning). Seeing a light several feet high upon Daci’s back, they thought he was a person of noble status.

Once he had been rescued, they vied with one another to give him clothing. When he was later summoned to be served a meal and spoken to, they gradually became familiar with him and realized he was merely a village elder.
They then questioned him about the origin of the light, to which he replied, "I have recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for fifty years."

That which was carried on one's back was a sūtra. There were no calamities or hardships, whether before or after, from which he did not escape; this was known to be the power of the sūtra (from the *Baoying ji*).
By Yi Lun of the Song dynasty.
Tang Sengyilun served as the Administrative Assistant (Dianqian) of the Guo Prince’s household during the Linde era. He died suddenly and was restored to life after three days, saying:
"I was summoned and saw the King of Yama, who said: 'You once killed dogs, rabbits, and pigeons; you are now being prosecuted for this. Your lifespan was destined to end.
However, I have just seen that your teacher told me you recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; not only will this extinguish your sins, but it shall also extend your years. I...
"I now release you. Can you refrain from consuming wine and meat and maintain the recitation of the Honored Scripture? Yi Lun bowed in thanks and replied, "I can.
He then saw a monk upon a bed inside the hall, appearing to be fifty or sixty years of age and wearing a *kāṣāya*. Yi Lun immediately prostrated himself before him. The monk said, "I am your teacher;
that is why I have come to save you. You may follow the King's words. Yi Lun replied, "Yes. The King then gave his command.
Following the messenger, he went to inspect the hells. Upon first entering one location, he saw large cauldrons arranged in rows, with fires burning beneath them;
within the cauldrons, people were being boiled, their cries of agony so heart-rending as to evoke profound pity. Entering yet another location, he saw iron beds that were exceedingly wide.
A person lay upon it, scorched and blackened until their features could no longer be distinguished. To the west, three withered and black figures stood upright;
they somewhat resembled women. They knelt before Yilun and said, "We have not been able to eat for several hundred years.
Lun replied, "I myself have nothing; how can I give it to you? He then entered another prison and said to the wardens, "It is very hot."
Fearing that his family would see him and prepare his funeral rites, he departed. After walking several dozen paces toward the southwest, he called out, "I have no official documents;

I fear the gatekeeper will not let me pass. He then obtained three lines of vermilion writing, none of which he could recognize. The gatekeeper indeed questioned him, and after he had read them, the man was released.
Thereupon he regained consciousness (from the *Baoying ji*).
Yang Fugong’s younger brother was a Tang palace eunuch surnamed Yang; his personal name has been forgotten. He was the younger brother of Fugong.

For more than twenty years, he remained within the rebel camps of Qin Zongquan, Lu Yanhong, and Liu Jurong. He did nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Although he stayed inside the city walls, he never once...
[Li] Fei was dismissed. Zongquan’s son was appointed as the Regional Commander (Jiedushi) of Xiangyang, with Yang serving as the Military Supervisor (Jianjunshi).

Taking advantage of the people’s state of fear and anxiety, Yang incited his subordinate general Zhao Deyan to attack and kill Zongquan’s son, then issued a proclamation appointing Deyan as the Regional Commander.
Consequently, the military administration gradually stabilized, and the people returned to their former livelihoods. As for Yang’s recitation of scriptures—

He redoubled his efforts with even greater diligence. Once, while he was burning incense and reciting scriptures beneath a willow tree outside the commander’s gate, a scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* inscribed in golden characters suddenly flew down from the sky. Yang bowed, received it, and stood there, his mind and eyes struck with awe.
He thought, "Is this not a virtuous reward obtained through the power of my sincere faith? Thus, he remained among the rebel faction for twenty days.
That he was ultimately able to capture the great thief at the end of the year, establish extraordinary merit, and preserve his fortune and rank—
this was surely due to the secret protection of the Buddha (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Dong Jinzhao, Dong Jinzhao!

During the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he entered the military. At that time, while on night duty atop a tower to the east of the city, one moonlit night, he suddenly saw four men dressed in yellow approaching from the east.
They gathered and stood beneath the tower, stating their own names; their appearance was as if they were pursuing him.
They were captured. Thereupon they said to one another, "Dong Jinchao constantly recites the Diamond Sūtra; he dedicates a portion of its merit to protect the underworld authorities on our behalf.
We have received his kindness—how can we kill him? We must wait for him to meet with an unjust death. If this man escapes, [we shall be lost]."
"We have no one to rely upon," they said. One among them remarked, "Opposite Dong Jinchao’s door lives a man of the same age and the same surname, whose life span is equal to his own;
he can serve as a substitute. Having said this, the man suddenly vanished. Jinchao was struck with wonder.

When morning came, he heard the sound of wailing from the house opposite his door. Upon asking the reason, the parents of the deceased said, "Our son died suddenly last night. Jinchao was further amazed.
In the morning, he was moved to tears as he recounted these events; he subsequently provided for her funeral and burial, and made offerings to his mother.
Later, he left the household life, taking the Dharma name Huītong and residing at Xingyuan Temple (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Kāng Zhòngqì, Kāng Zhòngqì.
In the eleventh year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty, he went to Hǎidōng and did not return for several years. His mother had an only son;

as days turned into months, she grew weary with longing. A monk came to beg for food, and the mother told him her story in detail. The monk said, "Simply recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."

The son was ill and was about to return. His mother could not read characters, so she had him copy out a scripture; she then hollowed out a pillar of the house to bury it and applied lacquer over the top.
Morning and evening, she paid it reverent homage. One night, a great thunderclap struck, uprooting this pillar and carrying it away. More than a month later, the son indeed returned.
He brought a massive log home, contained within a silk pouch, and upon entering, he bowed and knelt before his mother. When his mother questioned him, he replied, "It was my second kinsman."
He said, "At sea, my boat was wrecked by a storm and I fell into the water. Suddenly, there was a clap of thunder, and I threw this wood onto the waves.
I then used it to float myself to shore. My life is what this [wood] granted me; how could I not revere it? His mother cried out in alarm, saying:
"It must be a pillar of our treasury of scriptures. He then broke the pillar and obtained the scripture; mother and son constantly recited it together (*from the Baoying ji*).
Wu Kejiu, Wu Kejiu, was a native of Yue. In the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he resided in Chang'an and followed the Maṇi teachings. His wife was Wang.

The man also followed her advice. After more than a year, his wife died suddenly. Three years later, she appeared in a dream to her husband and said, "I have become a snake due to my wrong views and am now beneath the stupa at Huangzi Pond.
I shall die tomorrow morning; I pray that you will request a monk to go there and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, so that I may hope to escape this suffering.
The husband, not believing her in his dream, rebuked her. Enraged, the wife spat in his face, and he woke up in a start.

Jue’s face became swollen and painful beyond endurance. His wife again dreamed that her husband’s elder brother said to her, "Go to the garden, take some dragon-tongue grass (*nāgavallī*), pound it, and apply it as a poultice;
he will be cured immediately. Upon waking, the brother ran to fetch the grass and gave it to his younger brother. He was soon healed.

The following morning, the brothers went together to invite a monk to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Suddenly, a large snake emerged from within the stupa, raised its head, and gazed intently at the sutra until the end.
He died [of this illness] and was able to return to the Buddha for a long time; he constantly upheld this sutra (from the *Baoying ji*).
Regarding the monk Fazheng:
during the Kaiyuan era at the Prajñā Cloister of Jiangling Kaiyuan Temple, the monk Fazheng recited the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* twenty-one times every day.

At the beginning of the Changqing era, he fell ill and passed away. Upon arriving at the Office of the Netherworld, he saw someone who appeared to be a king. The king asked what meritorious deeds the Master had performed throughout his life.

He replied, "I constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Thereupon, the king gestured for him to ascend the hall; he climbed the embroidered throne and recited the sutra seven times.
All the attendants joined their palms below the steps, and all interrogations and punishments ceased as they listened. When the recitation was finished, the king dispatched an official.
As he was being led back, the king descended the steps to see him off, saying, "Venerable sir, you shall remain among men for another thirty years; do not neglect your recitation and study.
Thereupon, he followed the official for several tens of li until they reached a great pit. The official then leaned over the edge of the pit and pushed him from behind.
If he had fallen from the sky, seven days after his death, only his face remained warm.
The monk Changjing of Jingzhou personally witnessed this event (from the Youyang zazu).
The Śrāmaṇera Dàoyìn of Shíshǒu County, Táng: There was a śrāmaṇera named Dàoyìn who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Early in the Chángqìng era, while returning home at night after having gone out, he suddenly encountered a tiger roaring and lunging forward on the road. Knowing he could not escape, the śrāmaṇera closed his eyes and sat down.
He silently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, vowing in his heart to rescue and protect [the tiger]. The tiger then lay down in the grass to guard him.

At dawn, when people from the village began to pass by, the tiger departed. When he looked at the place where the tiger had crouched, its saliva was found flowing upon the ground (from the *Youyang zazu*).
He was called He Lao, a native of Ezhou who had long been a merchant. He specialized in the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

During the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, while traveling at night with his goods carried by hired laborers, he fell into a deep sleep on a mountain path. Suddenly, one of the laborers seized him by the neck and threw him into a mountain ravine.
Having taken his goods, he was hurrying to the market just as he was about to sell them when he saw the old man He approaching. He was filled with great terror.
He said, "By the power of my recitation of the sutras, I have vowed not to speak of this to anyone. Thereupon, they became monks together (*from the *Baoying ji*).
Gulong Yi. Gulong Yi was a native of Langzhou. During the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, he supported himself by working as a laborer in Qixian County.

Once, while going to visit a fellow villager who was ill, he saw that the man had transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. For no apparent reason, Gulong Yi defaced it and stopped him from continuing.
He cut it off. Upon returning home, he immediately became mute and speechless. Physicians could not cure him. Stubborn, ignorant, and lacking discernment, he still did not repent in the end.
After only five or six years, he suddenly heard a neighbor reciting this sutra. He was struck with a sense of urgency and reproached himself, saying:

"In the past, I slandered the true sutra and incurred this disease of muteness. If I were now to repent and apologize, and venerate it for the rest of my life, would I then be able to speak again? From that time on, every...

Whenever he heard someone reciting the sutras, he would lean against the wall and listen with single-minded concentration. After more than a month, he began to suspect that he had learned them by heart.
One day, while walking into a temple, he encountered an elderly monk whom he greeted with a bow. When the monk asked what was the matter, he pointed to his mouth to indicate that he was mute.

The monk then used a knife to cut beneath his tongue, whereupon he was immediately able to speak. Consequently, when he recited the sutras, his voice was exactly like that of his neighbor; this continued for some time.
He went to visit a monk, but could no longer find him; he thereafter worshipped a mural painting of Subhūti for the rest of his life (from the *Baoying ji*).
Zhao An, Zhao An—native of Chengdu—during the fourth year of the Dàhé era of the Táng dynasty, regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* ten times daily. At that time, the Mán...

When the invaders retreated, Hui’an encountered military equipment along the road and immediately collected it to store in his home. He was denounced by those who bore him a grudge, and the officials arrived at his gate to arrest him.
Weeping and prostrating himself before the scriptures, he departed; however, he was seized by the jailers and subsequently falsely confessed to the crime.

He was about to be sentenced when he arrived at the Commander’s hall; his cangue and shackles fell away of their own accord. The Commander then interrogated him. Hui’an said, “I am not a thief; I obtained everything from the streets and alleys.
It is likely due to the power of my recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Commander scolded him, refusing to believe him.
After passing the next day, he suddenly wrote the character "fang" (release) beneath the name "An," followed by the words, "The rest shall all follow the rule.

He did not know what this meant at all. Upon his return, he bathed and paid homage to the scriptures. When he opened the case to look inside, the sutras were crumpled, torn, and their rollers broken, as if they had been crushed by a strong man.
His wife said, "I suddenly heard a sound from within the case, as if there were someone striking or hacking at it."
Thus, when he was subjected to interrogation and examination, there was no discrepancy [in his testimony] (from the *Baoying ji*).
As for Ning Mian:
Ning Mian was a man from Yunzhong. In his youth, he possessed great courage; he was skilled in horsemanship and archery, and was able to subdue fierce beasts with his bare strength.
He did not employ weapons. The Governor of Beidu admired his courage and appointed him as a military commander (*yājiàng*). Later, he led four thousand troops to station at Feihu City.
At that time, the Commander of Jimen was arrogant and tyrannical; he abandoned the laws of the Son of Heaven, and a letter of rebellion reached the imperial court.
Emperor Wenzong of the Tang issued an edict for the Governor of Beidu to attack him from the south. Before the edict had even arrived, the troops of Jimen launched a night assault.
At Feihu, the gongs and drums shook the earth. The people of Feihu were in a state of agitation and felt no sense of security.
They said to Ning Mian, "The Ji troops are fierce and robust; they cannot be resisted. They are now about to arrive, and their momentum is extremely urgent. We pray that you empty the city and flee."
Otherwise, they will pull down my city by morning or evening. I cannot bear to see my father, sons, and brothers all fall beneath the blades of these rebels;
once it is too late, what regret can avail? Though the Son of Heaven possesses divine martial prowess, how could he possibly clear away my grievances? I pray you consider this carefully.

Although I am constrained by the small number of my troops and cannot withstand the vanguard of the army from Ji, I shall listen to the words of the local people, fearing that [otherwise] I might incur their offense.
The Son of Heaven wished to strengthen his defenses and hold the city, yet he feared that the people of the entire district would all be slaughtered by the hands of the rebels.

His anxiety was extreme, yet he could not decide upon a course of action. Suddenly, a spy reported: "The rebels have been completely routed; there are discarded armor and equipment beneath the city walls;

please go and retrieve them. He hurriedly ascended the city wall to look out. At that time, the moon was bright and clear, and he saw the rebel troops fleeing in disarray. They were stumbling and falling.
Those who were brought down by him were beyond counting. When a large army struck from behind, Yuan Mian was greatly cheered;
he opened the city gates and unleashed his troops to pursue them, capturing dozens of men alive and seizing a great quantity of abandoned armor.

Previously, Mian had been fond of the Buddhists and often read Buddhist scriptures, such as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. After defeating the Ji commandery forces, he captured their prisoners and interrogated them. The captives said: "This evening..."
Looking up at the city wall, he saw several giants, over twenty feet tall, both majestic and terrifying. With eyes blazing in anger and mouths agape, they stood bare-chested and grasping swords.
When the people of Ji saw them, they were struck with horror and trembled with sweat as they fled to hide; how could they have had any intention of fighting?
Yuan Mian realized that these giants were actually Vajrapāṇis and marveled at this even more. Yuan Mian later served as the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Yushi Zhongcheng).
Later, he served as an assistant commissioner for the Qing Sai (as recorded in the *Xuānshì Zhì*).
Ní Qín was a native of Zǐzhōu. In the fifth year of the Dàhé era of the Táng dynasty, he was renowned for his military prowess; consequently, he took charge of Xìngjiào in Fúzhōu.
Cang had long been a practitioner of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. His main hall faced the river and was a place of great scenic beauty;
