His brilliance illuminated the world, yet he was pitied for his short lifespan, which lasted but thirty-one years; at the age of twenty-nine, he ceased his lectures.

Thereupon, he searched the Tripitaka and obtained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He devoted himself with utmost sincerity to its recitation, prostrating before the Buddha and performing repentance, never ceasing day or night.

When the time of his death arrived, he suddenly heard a voice from the air saying: "Your life span was originally exhausted, but by the power of the merit of the *Prajñā*, you have attained [extension]."
His lifespan was doubled. Later, when he encountered those who had previously seen him, they were struck with wonder and could not fathom it.
He concealed the reason for this, but only then did they realize that the power of the sutra is inconceivable (from the *Zimencunxing lu*).

Li Qiuyi of the Tang dynasty was fond of hawks, dogs, and hunting. In the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, while serving as the Assistant Magistrate of Gaoyou in Yangzhou, he suddenly died one day from a violent illness.
He saw two men come to pursue him; one of them said his surname was Duan. At that time, they were together... [text fragment ends]
There were over a hundred pursuers; the men were all placed in cangues, while the women were bound hand and foot behind their backs. Qiu alone was shackled and led at the front.
After traveling about ten li, they saw several dozen large locust trees with horse troughs beneath them.

Duan said, "The Great Deity of the Five Paths always stops his horse here to inspect the merits and faults of those among humans. Only then did Qiu realize that he was dead. They arrived at the gate of the King.
Duanzhi said to one of the attendants, "This man is surnamed Jiao and named Ce; he is your original leader. He was then brought before the King.
The King said, "How could you be so cruel and devoid of kinship? You took pleasure in killing the lives of others for your own enjoyment.

In an instant, all the beasts and birds he had killed appeared and spoke in human voices, saying, "We beg for an early judgment. Jiao Ce stepped forward and said, "Qiu Yi does not yet deserve to die."
The King asked, "What merit had you previously performed? He replied, "I once transcribed a single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The King then joined his palms and said, "In the netherworld, the *Vajracchedikā* is proclaimed as the supreme merit; since you were able to transcribe it, your fortune is no small matter.
He immediately ordered Jiao Ce to lead him toward the scripture repository to verify this. Upon arriving at a jeweled hall filled with various scriptures, Qiu tested [him].
He drew out one scroll and found it was indeed the scripture he had composed. Upon returning to see the king, he knew his creation was authentic.

The king then summoned the creatures he had killed and ordered them to offer a sincere apology; he granted permission for merit to be performed on their behalf. Qiu followed the king’s command exactly, vowing to transcribe one hundred scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The multitude dispersed in great joy, and the king said, "Let them go. Jiao Ce led them out through the city gate, saying: [The remainder of the text follows.]

He exerted himself to such an extent; how could he not have been repaid? Qiu offered him three hundred thousand coins, but he would not accept them. Instead, he provided funds to produce twenty volumes of scriptures.
When they reached a pit, [the monk] pushed against it with his staff and was revived. He had been inside the coffin for three days, hearing only the sound of wailing.
People were summoned in alarm, and when the coffin was broken open, he rose up. Within ten days, he finished transcribing twenty scrolls of scripture. His body was scorched...
Chè came to express his gratitude and departed after delivering his message. He soon completed the hundred fascicles as well.
The Governor of Yangzhou reported this matter to the throne, and by imperial decree, Qiu was granted the fifth rank and appointed as the Pacification Commissioner of Xizhou (from the *Baoying ji*).
Yu Chang of the Tang dynasty served as the Recorder (Lùshì Cānjūn) of Bingzhou during the reign of Empress Wu. Every time after the first watch, he would gasp for breath and break into a sweat;
by the second watch, he would recover. His wife, Lady Liu, was about to summon a physician when Yu Chang said secretly, "I have no ailment."
It was arduous; he settled legal affairs by day and adjudicated matters in the underworld by night, until his strength could no longer sustain him.

Whenever he learned of impending calamities, he would secretly make preparations for them, never revealing a word. This continued for six years. Later, when his mother passed away, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He was no longer reborn as a minister of the underworld. Because he had spoken extensively of the power of these meritorious deeds, he caused his descendants to wear and turn [the beads].
Later, serving as the *Simā* (Governor) of Qingzhou, at the age of eighty-four, as he was about to pass away, he suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance unlike anything found in this world.
He said to those around him, "A sage is coming to welcome me to the Western Land. Having finished speaking, he passed away. (From the *Baoying ji*).
Pei Xuanli was a native of Tang.
During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, he served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Land. He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Once, while imprisoned for an offense, Xuanli was overcome with anxiety; however, by reciting the sutra with single-minded devotion, his shackles and fetters were suddenly released on their own. The investigating official personally visited him to investigate the matter.
Consequently, he was exonerated. The Censor Ren Zhi was imprisoned together with him; by reciting the sutra, he too was spared (from the *Baoying ji*).
Wu Sixuan of the Tang dynasty served as a University Doctor during the reign of Empress Wu. He believed in the Śākya teachings and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily.

He recited it twice daily, and there were many miraculous responses. Later, he grew somewhat lax, performing it only once a day. While Si-xuan was ill in the capital, the sorcerer Chu Xi-er could divine matters with godlike accuracy.
When Si-xuan went down to the stars to pray for his ailment, he visited Xi-er. Upon seeing him, Xi-er was startled and said:
"What does the Duke have? Upon seeing him, the ghosts all fled. Sīxuān secretly realized this was due to the scripture;

he therefore redoubled his diligent efforts and recited it five times every day. His elder brother fell ill, and the physicians were ineffective. Sīxuān recited the scripture with a sincere heart, and after three days, his brother recovered.
Once, at the Wei Bridge, Sīxuān saw an old man over eighty years of age wearing coarse mourning clothes. He questioned him, saying:

She was the mother who gave birth to him. He contemplated this as a profound mystery and replied: "When my mother was forty-three years old, a strange monk instructed her, saying, 'Do you wish for long life?
Simply recite the Diamond Sutra. Thereupon, my mother resolved her mind and recited it twice."

Originally [she was] one hundred and seventy; when her neighbor’s mother recited [the scriptures], she surpassed the age of one hundred. Now, following her mother’s practice, she is already ninety years old (from the *Baoying ji*).
Xue Shaoyin.
Xue Shaoyin of Hedong was a candidate for the jinshi examination. One day, he suddenly died of a sudden illness in Chongyi Ward in Chang’an.

An official arrived carrying a document stating, "The Great Officer summons you to be led away. Upon entering the gate of the government office, those who saw him recognized it as the residence of Xianyu Shuming.
Shaoyin wished to lodge a complaint, but Shuming said, "The Cold Food Festival is approaching; why are you carving chickens?"
It was Zi Shi’s turn to eat. To the east sat a monk holding a precious pagoda-fan that opened into two parts; Shao Yin was already seated within it.
Shu Ming said, "I was just about to report this matter to the Abbot; why did you rescue this man? He then forced him out and ordered him to be led before the Judge.
Upon reaching the west courtyard, the gatekeeper went inside to announce him. After a brief hesitation...
Upon hearing this command, he dressed in plain garments and entered. What he saw was his deceased elder brother.

They wept together for a long time, and the brother said, "I thought that since you had not yet achieved fame, I wished to recommend you here to share in the affairs of the Lord. Therefore, I feigned a visit from the underworld; it was for no other reason.
I have recently married in the world of the dead and am truly reluctant to remain. His brother said, "In my same courtyard is an official named Wang, whose office is located in the West..."
"Cao, since you have come here, you may pay him a visit before departing. He then ordered Shao Yin to see him at the western courtyard. Shao Yin received him with great hospitality.
Suddenly, the sound of preparations for a meal was heard, with every variety of land and sea delicacies fully provided. Before they had eaten, Official Wang suddenly rose and looked back.
Seeing the monk who had previously carried the stupa, he said, "You must not eat this; if you eat it, there will be no way to return. Shao Yin replied:
"How can we endure such extreme hunger? the monk replied, "Only honey-fried ginger may be eaten. They took it and ate it, yet the official Wang did not arrive at all.
The monk said, "You may go now. Shortly thereafter, Yao Shao-yin emerged again; he went to his elder brother, weeping and entreating him to let him leave.

The elder brother knew he could not be detained and entered to inform the local government, which granted permission. Shao-yin said, "Now that I have been allowed to return to the human world, I wish for you to know [this]."
"What office will you hold? His elder brother said, "This is difficult to say; what use is it to know?
Despite his earnest request, the brother summoned a clerk to retrieve and examine the registers, yet he would not let him see them. He said, "It is only next year that you shall achieve success.

At first, you will obtain it in the far west. Thereafter, you will serve as a district magistrate and a county sheriff. Then there will be another post in the extreme south. Beyond this, I cannot know."
Upon their parting, the elder brother said, "I have sent my former attendant, Li Jun, to accompany you; should you encounter any peril, you may rely upon him.
Once they had departed, whenever they encountered a moment of danger, they would see that monk leading the way before them. Shaoyin asked, "Disciple, we have never been acquainted before;
why does the Master protect me in such a manner? The monk replied, "I am holding the *Vajra* for you."
Because of this, they protected one another. Ya Xing recounted the matter in detail. In the spring of the following year, he indeed passed the imperial examination.

Before long, he was appointed as a Corrector of Scribes in the Secretariat and served as an Envoy for Pacifying the Barbarians. Upon his return, he was transferred to the post of Magistrate of Tongguan.

When his term expired, he encountered Zhao Chang, who had become the Regional Inspector of Annam. Since Xiao Yin had an old friendship with Zhao, he requested that Zhao appoint him as an official attendant, wishing to avoid [the hardships of] the journey.

When he was an official in the South, Chang Xu told him, "I have not yet had the leisure to submit a memorial for you as a regional commander. Upon reaching Jiangling, I shall petition with a memorial on your behalf.
When the memorial arrived, Yao Xin soon thereafter encountered the mourning period for his mother; once his term of mourning ended, he was selected and appointed as the County尉 (wei) of Wannian.
At that time, a soldier of Qingzi fought and died with a page from the Prince of Fu’s household. The Jingzhao Prefecture failed to report this to Emperor Dezong, who became violently incensed.
At that moment, Shaoyin, the Lord of Jie, cautioned Tang; consequently, on one day, [Tang] was demoted to the post of Magistrate of Leize County in Gaizhou.
For over ten years, he underwent every kind of hardship, yet Li Jun constantly protected him. When Shunzong ascended the throne, an imperial edict was issued to recall him.
Shao Yin recorded the demoted officials. When he reached Guiyang with Li Ding, who was also a demoted official, they halted their horses by the water and spoke with an attendant;
it was Li Jun. Shao Yin said, "The appointed month and day have already expired.
My elder brother says that his official tenure ends here. Since Li Jun is departing again, it will not be long [before our time is up]. Li Ding was startled.
He lamented the matter and questioned him; [the monk] told him everything in detail. A few days later, he passed away (from the *Xianding lu*).
As for Lu Bian:
his elder brother served as the Magistrate of Hucheng. Bian was traveling from the Eastern Capital to the provincial office when he stayed overnight at the Second Valley.
In a dream, he saw two officials dressed in yellow robes coming to pursue him. They traveled until they reached a certain place with city walls.
After entering the city, they were about to pass by the Judge when an envoy arrived. The Judge went out to welcome him, and the officials led [the dreamer] to stay at a residence below.
Above that house was a roof-covering, but there were no beams or pillars beneath it. Below were ten large millstones, and beside the stones were several hundred women.
The millstone rotated by itself. More than ten ox-headed executioners used a large winnowing basket to scoop up women and place them within the hole of the mill;
they emerged with their flesh and bones pulverized. The sound of their agonizing pain was unbearable to hear. Within the crowd, Bian saw his paternal aunt, who was the wife of Hu Cheng.
Upon seeing one another, they were filled with both grief and joy, and each asked the other the reason for their presence there. Bian said:
"What kind of retribution are these beings suffering? he asked. [The official] replied, "They have reached this state because they sat idly while harboring jealousy.
Bian said, "What can be done about it? His aunt-in-law said, "You have always maintained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Try reciting it for me; perhaps it will extinguish their sins.

Because Bian then recited the sutra, the millstone ceased to turn and the suffering of those undergoing retribution subsided slightly. A ox-headed executioner holding a fork approached Bian and said angrily:
"What business has a young master come here to recite sutras and save people? Bian replied, "My paternal aunt is here.
The executioner said, "If you cherish your aunt, you may take her with you. Bian then led his aunt away and fled the city; they each returned to their own lives.
Initially, Bian had only one small servant accompanying him who had been dead for half a day; that servant was now about to return and report the news.
After Bian had revived, several days later he arrived at Hucheng. Upon entering the gate, he encountered Bian’s elder brother, who was performing a *zhai* (fasting) ritual.

When the family members saw Bian, they were filled with joy and surprise and went back to report it. His elder sister-in-law came forward to meet him, took his hand, and said, "Had I not met you, I would have entered the millstone.
That I am now reborn is due to your power. (From the *Guang yiji*).

Regarding Qian'er Han-guang, the County Vice-Magistrate of Zhushan: His wife, Lady Lu, had died half a year prior. When Han-guang’s term of office ended, he returned home and resided at Zhushan Temple.
There was a large mound there; one day while gazing out from it during a moment of leisure, he suddenly saw Lady Lu by the side of the mound.
They met and wept with joy; he asked about the circumstances of his death, whereupon [the spirit] gazed northward and saw a great city, saying, "My residence is here.
He invited Huángguāng to go with him, and they entered the city. The buildings within the city were magnificent and grand, no different from those in the human world.
Beside it was a courtyard. Within the courtyard, proceeding westward, were several dozen rooms; the Lu family resided in the third room.

Their marital affection remained no different than usual, and their clothing, amusements, and furnishings were likewise so. After some time had passed, as evening fell, she said to Han-guang, "The underworld is strict and severe;
you should return for now. You may bring your children here another day, for I wish to have something [discussed] with them."

[He] instructed him: "Do not trouble yourself to come tomorrow. On the following day, Hanguang went again. When the Lu family saw him, they were struck with astonishment and said, "We cautioned you not to come;
how could you have arrived once more? Shortly thereafter, an official in crimson robes arrived at the monastery accompanied by dozens of attendants.
The Lu family ordered Hanguang to enter beneath the bed and lowered a felt curtain to the ground to shield him from view, instructing him to remain there.
"Do not look! I fear that host and guest might commit some transgression. Suddenly, she heard someone outside calling for "Lu Siniang. Lu stepped out;
at first, Han Guang was terrified, but later she stole glances. In the courtyard, there were twenty-eight women dressed in vermilion robes, each ordered to undo their hair-knots.
They were tied in pairs and cast into a cauldron. The sounds of their agonizing cries could be heard for several li. Only when the fire was extinguished did it cease.
She departed. Lady Lu hurried straight into her room. When Faheng saw her enter, he took her hand and placed it upon the bed; she remained unconscious for a long while.
Upon regaining consciousness, Faheng asked why she was undergoing such suffering again, given her lifelong practice of vegetarianism, reciting sutras, and chanting the Buddha’s name.

She replied, "In the past, when I was about to die, a monk came to see me and asked me to transcribe the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*. At that time, I gave my word to do so, though my illness was already critical."
In my haste, I forgot his final instructions; for this I am receiving the retribution for lying and suffering such a cruel punishment.
My desire to see my son was precisely so that he might create a copy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. Now that you have seen it, there is no need for my son to do so.
Hanguang returned home and recounted the matter to his sons in full; they wept bitterly throughout the night. When dawn broke, they went to look, but he was already gone.
He looked again and saw nothing but overgrown weeds. He then sold his family assets to obtain five hundred thousand coins;

the Provincial Governor and those below him each provided further assistance so that the total reached two thousand guan. He then ordered his eldest son to carry the scriptures to Mount Wutai to copy them.

Upon reaching the mountain, he traveled throughout all the terraces but had not yet found a permanent residence. Shortly thereafter, while ascending the mountain path halfway up the terrace, he encountered an old man.

A monk said to him, "You have copied scriptures to save your mother; why do you linger so long? Leave the money on the altar and you should return quickly to copy the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Having spoken, he vanished. The son realized this was Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; he left the money and returned.
When he had finished copying the sutra and left the platform, he again saw a hell. He entered directly, but finding the gate closed, he knocked upon it.
From within, a voice asked, "Who is it? Zhanfu of the Commandery replied, "It is I.
After a long time, a woman emerged and said, "I thank your noble lord for the power of copying this sutra; you have already attained rebirth in the human realm. Please take great care of yourself."
Chong asked, "Why does Lady Han-guang reside here? She replied, "My offenses are largely similar to hers;
that is why I am here as well. (From the *Guang yiji*).

Wang Tuo was a *guoyi* (cavalry officer) in the Yin-yang Bureau. Due to illness, he subsequently abstained from pungent foods and vegetables. He resolved his mind to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* five times daily.
Later, he contracted a malarial fever and saw a host of ghosts approaching. Tuo immediately and urgently recited the sutra; upon hearing it, the ghosts...

The ghost retreated and said from afar, "The King has ordered you to be pursued; cease reciting the sutra for now. Da-tuo immediately stopped. The ghosts all moved forward, and Da-tuo then fell into a stupor, on the verge of death.
After a short while, he saw another ghost come and say, "O reciter of the sutra, the King has granted you a temporary reprieve of six months.
Upon waking, he resolved to maintain his recitation with single-minded devotion, never ceasing day or night. Although the six months had passed, the ghosts did not appear.
Later, at night, he heard a voice in the air calling out: "By virtue of your merit from upholding this sutra, your lifespan shall reach ninety years.
It turned out exactly as the voice had said (from the *Baoying ji*).

Wang Lingwang, a prince of the Tang, had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since his youth. While returning to Qiongzhou, he encountered a path by a stream that was extremely treacherous and perilous.
Suddenly, he met a fierce beast; overcome with extreme terror, he hurriedly recited the true scripture. The beast stared at him intently, then trailed its tail and departed, drooling saliva.
Mandi served as the Administrative Assistant (Panshi) of Anzhou. While crossing the Yangtze River, a violent wind arose at night;

hundreds of hired boats following one after another were all submerged, yet only the boat commanded by Liang Wang remained intact. He later died as the Magistrate of Qiao in Bozhou (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).

He Jingtang, whose secular surname was He, served as the Magistrate of Wude in Huai Prefecture during the early Tianshou era. He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Once, when he reached Heyang, the river rose and the bridge collapsed;

it was already evening, and people were scrambling onto boats. Before he could reach the bank, he was on the verge of drowning. Terrified, He Jingtang— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly at "He Jingtang," leaving the narrative incomplete.)
He urgently recited a sutra. In a brief moment, he reached the shore and encountered hanging reeds; by climbing them, he escaped.
The other eighty-odd people drowned (from the *Baoying ji*).

Zhang Xuansu was a native of Luoyang during the Tang dynasty. In his youth, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. At the beginning of the Tiānshòu era, he served as the magistrate of Huángméi.

When his family encountered a calamity, it was dispelled by the mere thought of the scripture. At the age of seventy, he fell ill; suddenly, a flowered canopy appeared suspended in the sky, whereupon he bathed himself.
He took his leave of his family while bathing and suddenly passed away (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).

As for the Tian family, there was the family of Tian, a military officer (*cānjiān*) of Yizhou, who by nature delighted in hunting; he constantly kept hawks and dogs as his primary occupation during the early Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty.
In Yizhou, while releasing a hawk upon a thicket of brambles, he saw a scroll of scripture. Taking it and looking at it, he found it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
From that time on, he resolved his mind to recite it; after several years, he had already recited it more than two thousand times.
Nevertheless, he did not cease hunting. Later, he fell ill and died suddenly; after several days, he was summoned to the Underworld. There he saw various birds and beasts surrounding him in numbers.
Mǔ followed Jǐ to receive his summons. After a short while, he arrived and saw the King; when asked why his offenses were so numerous, Mǔ was unable to respond.
The King ordered an official to take him away for interrogation. His ten companions reached the administrative office, where the clerk ordered them to open their mouths.

He threw a pill into each of their mouths, and instantly a blazing fire erupted, spreading over their entire bodies. In a moment they were reduced to ashes, but shortly thereafter they were restored to human form once more.
In this manner, six or seven individuals reached the field of Mr. Tian. Although he rolled up three pellets in succession, no sign of fire appeared.
The official found this strange and led him again into the presence of the King. He reported the facts in full. The King asked what meritorious deeds he had performed while alive.
Mr. Tian replied, "At first, I made my living by hunting. The King questioned him further, and he said, "During my lifetime, I found gold on thorns in Yizhou."
She had already recited the Diamond Sūtra more than two thousand times. The King said, "This very act shall extinguish all her sins.

He ordered his attendants to check the register of merits for the Tian family, and they returned with a report exactly as he had said. The King then personally instructed the lady Tian to recite the sūtra;

after only three sheets, she looked back into the courtyard and saw that the birds and beasts were no longer there. When the recitation was finished, the King praised her, saying, "To have recited it two thousand times!"
His life was extended by fifteen years, and he was subsequently permitted to return home (*from the Guǎngyìjì*).

Lǐ Wúyàn, the Magistrate of Jiàndé County, had maintained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since his youth. Toward the end of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, Wúyàn was serving as... [remainder of text omitted].

Yao served as a military aide (*canjun*) in the commandery. When his term of office expired, he was returning north and passed through Wuzhang Village. It happened that the embankment at Jiangdai in Shangyu had broken, leaving the water exhausted.
It was the middle of the night, pitch black and dark, with no one around for four miles. This road had long been notorious for bandits.
Since there were several hundred bolts of Wu brocade in Yan’s boat, he feared they would be seized by thieves; thus, he took a sword, went before the boat, and recited the sutras.
After the third watch, he saw two torches on the embankment approaching from afar. Yan alone suspected they were villagers coming to protect him;
when the torches reached a hundred paces from the boat, they retreated and turned back. He found this quite strange and redoubled his efforts, reciting the sutras with an even more forceful voice.
I also reflected to myself: "Could this not be due to the power of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? At that time, the water in the pond had dried up while the water outside was full.
The swallows, feeling at ease, thought to themselves, "If the pond breaks, we shall have the aid of the water.

After half the night had passed, they suddenly heard the sound of flowing water from the head of the boat. Startled, they cried out, "The pond is several zhang wide; how could it have broken? After a long while...
He felt the boat begin to float slightly. By dawn, the river was already full; directly opposite the boat, there was a hole several feet wide.

He then realized that reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* had been his aid. Wei Yan’s younger brother, Wei Yu, who served as the Vice Prefect of Chuzhou, saw that his elder brother had achieved merit through reciting the sutra and thus emulated him.
Later, while traveling by boat out of the gorges, the water became so swift that the oar broke and the boat was on the verge of capsizing.
He was defeated and fled. He then recited the sutra with all his might. Suddenly, he saw a boat oar floating down the current and was thus able to escape.
His kinsmen also regularly recited the Diamond Sutra. During the rebellion of An Lushan, they were hiding in the wild grasses.

As the rebels drew near, they thought of finding a pair of shoes to flee in. Suddenly, something fell upon their backs; looking up in alarm, they found it was a new pair of shoes (from the *Guang yiji*).
Sun Mingtang:
Sun Ming was a native of Yangwu in Zhengzhou. His family had been poor and lowly for generations; he served as a tenant farmer on the estate of Lu Shi.

He was skilled at reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, chanting it twenty times every day for twenty years. From the moment he first began reciting the sūtra, he had abstained from meat and strong-smelling foods.
Afterwards, while he was reciting with right mindfulness, he suddenly saw two officials come to pursue him. Mingyi thought they were county officials and went toward the county seat.
After traveling about five or six li, he arrived at the gate of a government office. The gatekeeper said, "The King has already gone on inspection.
Consequently, the official confined Mingyi in an empty room. That room extended fifty or sixty bays wide and was covered like a mass of clouds. Seven days passed. The King—
Just as they arrived, an official led Ming into the palace. The King asked, "What merit do you possess? He replied, "I have been reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for twenty years.
The King said, "This is a great merit. He then turned to his attendants and said, "Yesterday we received a formal document from the Jetavana Monastery."
The monk Ming pleaded earnestly for twenty more years of recitation, realizing that the cultivation of the Way is inconceivable;
these twenty years were requested to repay his meritorious efforts. He ordered an official to escort him back to his home.

His family had already completed the funeral rites for him, and although the spirit had returned to its body, the family members did not know it. It happened that a hunter passed by the tomb chamber and heard [Ming] crying out.

Sheng informed his family members, and because of this, they were able to survive. Toward the end of the Tianbao era, Ming had been alive for six or seven years and was in excellent health (from the *Guang yiji*).
The Three Swordsmen (Although they have already been recorded in the *Ganyingzhuan*, as the details differ, they are presented here again).
Regarding the Three Swordsmen of the Tang: their secular surname was Zhang and their given name was Boying. During the Qiannian era, he served as a soldier in Shouzhou.
Possessing the utmost filial piety, because his father was in Yingzhou, he stole an official horse to go and visit him. Upon reaching Huaiyin, he was...
The guards seized him and reported it to the Provincial Governor, Cui Zhao, who ordered that he be executed by decapitation outside the city walls.

At that time, the executioner was renowned for his skill with the blade; he struck twice, yet the victim’s body was not wounded at all. He then changed to a sharper blade and hacked with all his might, but the damage remained as before.
Startled, the executioner said, "When I strike with full force until my blade reaches his body, my hands feel weak. I do not know why. He immediately reported this to Cui Zhao.
When asked the reason for this, he replied: "In my youth, at fifteen, I once abstained from meat and blood and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for over ten years.

Since the onset of the chaos, however, I have been stationed within the army and no longer practiced recitation. Yesterday, because I was accused of an unfathomable crime, I resolved with all my heart to recite the sutra alone.
Zhaō sighed in admiration and let me go; I subsequently shaved my head to enter the monastic order and now wander for alms wearing large iron bells."

He prepared a vegetarian feast for a thousand people; it was all ready in a single day. People of the time called him the "Master of Three Knives," believing him to be the Bodhisattva Qijing (as recorded in the *Guang yi ji*).

Song Canjun was a Song official stationed in Fangzhou. In his youth, he had maintained the practice of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṇī*. When he took up his post, he temporarily resided in the quarters of the Office of Personnel (Sishu).
He already knew that the residence was ill-omened; therefore, every evening he would invariably recite the sutra. Suddenly, he saw a woman standing outside the door for a long time. Song—
He asked, "Are you not a ghost? She replied, "Yes. He asked again, "The realms of the unseen and the seen differ in principle;

it is not fitting for us to meet. Is there perhaps some grievance or injustice that has occurred? The woman then wept bitterly and said, "Indeed. I am the wife of the former Director of the Office of Personnel."
The Director of Personnel (Sishu) was on an official mission. His younger brother was coerced by him; he refused and did not comply, and for this reason he was killed.

The corpse was wrapped in felt and thrown into a latrine in the northwest corner of the hall. It became unbearable due to the accumulation of filth. Many people came wishing to lodge a complaint, but the laypeople were timid and cowardly;

upon seeing the form [of the ghost], they were inevitably struck with fear. Thus, their hidden grievances could not be made known, and the reports of these sudden, violent crimes reached the authorities.
"Maintaining this recitation shall serve as a great protection for all sentient beings. Seeing how she has been defiled by such filth, how could one not feel compassion for her?
Song Yun said, "At present my official rank is low, so I cannot save her alone. Tomorrow I will certainly petition the Magistrate on her behalf, and then the ghost will depart.
When dawn came, he reported in detail that they had dug up the earth and searched the latrine, yet had not found her corpse. As Song recited the sutra, the woman appeared once more.
Question: Why was it not obtained? Answer: It is only one chi away to the northwest; you should seek it there tomorrow to fulfill my kindness.
Following these words, he indeed obtained it; within the felt mat, only the bones remained. He washed them again and moved them to another location.
That evening he came again to offer his thanks. With great joy, the spirit said to him, "Your grace has been so profound that it is difficult to repay.
Although I dwell in the realm of darkness, there is still communication possible. You have two sons; the elder will be difficult to sustain, but the younger will surely continue your lineage."

Furthermore, he mentioned his honorable position and spoke of how the Song dynasty had subsequently altered official ranks and emoluments several times. He also said, "I am deeply ashamed before you, Governor;
I do not know how I might repay your kindness. When Song saw that the Governor had fully recounted their discussion, the Governor asked him what office he held at present.
When evening came, the woman appeared once more. She conveyed the messenger’s message, saying, "In one month you shall change offices, yet it will not be to your satisfaction;
you shall instead be appointed as a *biejia* (vice-governor) in Guizhou. Song reported these matters in detail, and all were verified. Initially, Song had asked:

"Since you have already been killed by someone, why do you not seek retribution? She replied: "The person who killed me is still currently serving in office; his life span has not yet reached its end. That is why..."
No further account has been recorded (from the *Guang yiji*).
As for Liu Hongjian:
Liu Hongjian was a clan nephew of the Grand Master of the Censorate, Zhang. At the beginning of the Qiannian era of the Tang dynasty, he encountered the chaos and migrated southward.
There was a monk who ordered him to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Hongjian recited the sūtra daily. In the first year of the Shangyuan era, he was staying in Shouchun.
One day, as he stepped out his door, he suddenly saw two officials who said, "We have come to summon you by order of the Grand Marshal.
Hongjian replied, "I do not know the Grand Marshal at all; why do you command me? He intended to resist, but the two officials suddenly came straight forward and dragged him away. Hongjian—
He gradually requested to put on his shirt, but the official refused to let him go. After being led along for no long time, they suddenly crossed the Huai River and arrived at a village.
In a moment, the official brought a hempen shirt and a waist-belt and ordered Hongjian to wear them, saying with a laugh, "This is truly a 'sour vinegar' great shirt.

Thereupon, they traveled northward; the road grew increasingly overgrown and difficult. Upon reaching a large city ahead, he entered it and found a government office that was most solemn and magnificent. Suddenly—
He saw the monk he had previously encouraged to recite the scriptures coming out from the office. A young attendant behind the monk recognized Hongjian;
he went straight to him and asked, "Young Master Shi, why have you come here? He then ran back to inform the Preceptor, saying, "The Sixteenth Young Master Liu has just been summoned by an official.
Since he has the merit of reciting the scriptures, would it not be right to rescue him thereby? Hongjian soon arrived at the monk's side.
He reverently prostrated himself and sought deliverance. The monk said, "I am your disciple; you shall suffer no harm. In a moment, an official led Li Hongjian into the hall.
Behind the desk stood a five-colored stupa, three or four feet high, which was spinning and rotating.

Before any interrogation could take place, the monk had already entered and questioned him. The stupa transformed into a handsome man about thirty years of age, who declared, "I am the Minister of the Interior."
He descended from his seat to receive the monk and asked, "Why has the Master returned? The monk replied, "Liu Hongjian is your own disciple.
His cultivation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* has reached such a high degree that his allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted; he ought to see you.
The King said, "If he has indeed cultivated the *Vajracchedikā*, I wish to hear it myself. He then ordered Liu to kneel and recite. After Hongjian had finished reciting two sheets of paper, suddenly—
He forgot [to take it]. To the west of the hall, there was a person holding a golden hook and a dragon-head banner (*dhvaja*).
Upon the banner, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was written in green characters and spread out before Hongjian. He was ordered to recite the sutra clearly;

when he had finished, the person vanished entirely, leaving only the halls and buildings in profound stillness. Consequently, he went out the door and saw only the pursuing officials. Suddenly, an object resembling two suns came and struck Hongjian.
Jian was like a wild goose gradually approaching; terrified, he fled in haste. Suddenly, he saw water by the side of the road.
Jian wished to stop and drink from it, but the pursuing officer said, "This is human fat. Only the surface is clear and pure, but beneath it is entirely nothing but leftover skin and putrid flesh."
He could not drink it and returned. A short while later, he arrived at his home and saw his skeletal form lying upon the bed; his heart was filled with deep sorrow.
A ghost pushed him from behind, and he entered the room as if in a trance. He subsequently revived, and the ghost departed only after receiving the money (from the *Guang yi ji*).

Shi Zu Nan of the Southern Song dynasty resided at Yunfeng on Mount Nanyue. He drew blood to transcribe five hundred fascicles of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, one hundred fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and ten sets of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. For twenty-seven years, he used his own blood for all these writings.

In his final years, his blood dried up and he became a mere skeleton of bone; yet the sound of him reciting the Buddha’s name never ceased. One day, while sitting in the abbot’s quarters, he passed away in the lotus position.
From between his eyebrows, śarīra relics burst forth, appearing one after another as soon as they were taken (as recorded in the *Fahua chizhanyu ji*).
Shi Mingxun, styled Mingxi, was a native of Hui. His original name was Hu Wenzhu. During the Tianqi era, he served as a Zhongshu Sheren (Secretariat Drafter).

Because he refused to transcribe the Confucian classics for Wei Zhongxian (the "Uei Dang"), he was ordered to be stripped of his official rank. Upon reaching the Bingxu year, he suddenly suffered from a facial ulcer whose pain was unbearable.
Ren (the patient) was in a state of fainting and delirium during the winter of the Xinmao year. He heard a voice from his wound speaking in human speech, saying: "I am Lady Lu of the Liang dynasty.
While in the palace in Luoyang, I met my death at the hands of bandits. More than six hundred years have passed since then, yet I still linger within the registers of the ghosts."
The person who murdered me on that very day has now been transformed into a man. You ought to transcribe sutras such as the Lotus Sūtra to exhort yourself and rescue me.

Wen Zhu, in his piteous prayer, began writing immediately upon feeling the pain. Residing in Yizhen at that time, he prepared paper and brushes and transcribed the Lotus Sūtra, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra, and other scriptures, as well as the Water Repentance Ritual. Every time he wrote, the pain [subsided].
He immediately stopped. As he set down his brush, the pain returned. After more than a year, he finished copying the scripture, and the ailment was finally cured.
In the summer of the *dingyou* year, I met Dui-shan at De-du, who recounted this matter in detail; however, it was not yet determined whether this referred to the Xiao Liang or the Zhu Liang dynasty.
The postscripts by scholars such as Li Ming-rui and Wang Yi-ding likewise failed to reach a definitive conclusion. Dui-shan said: "This is [from] the Zhu [Liang]."
It was the Liang dynasty. During the Xiao-Liang period, Luoyang belonged to the Wei. Furthermore, "Zhāoróng" (Imperial Concubine) is an official title from the Tang dynasty.
Thus, those who protected Emperor Zhaozong and were subsequently killed must have been either Zhu Yougui or Shi Shuzong. Having thus determined this, I inscribed it upon the register.
This was seen by Mr. Xue Cai, now known as the Daoist of Duishan. Recorded in the *Miji* (Notes on Rice). According to the research of Duishan: [End of Document]
This is most comprehensive. However, if this were the case, then the "Beiliang Palace Attendant" (Zhāoróng) would have to be the "Táng Palace Attendant" (Zhāoróng).

Alternatively, it may be that during Hu Jūn’s state of collapse [of consciousness], the sounds of "Táng" and "Liáng" were so close that they were corrupted; this cannot yet be known for certain (*Zhou Shíxù Zhì*).
Fang Zhu of Daizhou.
He once exhorted an elderly man to recite the Buddha’s name, and that man attained rebirth in the Western Pure Land.

Upon entering the underworld, he saw King Yama, who then released him back to the world, saying, "You shall be born in the Pure Land. Fang Zhu had [recited] ten thousand times the *Golden*... [text fragment].

I have made a vow to recite the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and also pay reverent homage at Mount Wutai; this heart’s desire has not yet been fulfilled, so I do not wish to be reborn [in the Pure Land] (as recorded in the *Ruìyìng shānchuán*).
Regarding Gu Yüantrǐ:
In the fifth year of the Zhengguān era of the Táng dynasty, there was one Gu Yüantrǐ, the Magistrate of Bāxī County in Lóngzhōu, who had faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma.

He wished to transcribe the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vajracchedikā*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and other sūtras, but having no means to verify his own work, he relied upon the Chan Master Kang of that land for proofreading.
Kang then transcribed the volumes according to the Dharma while staying at the monastery; they were then returned to his estate in Qizhou.
The scriptures remained at the estate, kept together with the five-thousand-word text of Laozi in one place. Suddenly, an external fire spread to them.
The hall was thatched with grass; when it burned, everything was reduced to ashes in an instant. At that time, Guitu happened to be serving as the magistrate of Renping County.

His family members called out to one another to sift through the ashes in search of the gold and copper rollers. Once they had sifted the ashes, they opened them to find that all the scriptures inside were intact, exactly as they had been before.
The color of the yellow silk remained unchanged; only the covers of the case were reduced to ashes. Furthermore, when they searched for the *Laozi*, it had already been consumed by fire.

At that time, all those who heard of or saw this, whether from distant or nearby villages, could not help but sigh in wonder at the marvel. As for the single fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the characters of its title were blackened by the fire.
Upon inquiring into the cause, it was found that when the scripture was first being titled, there was a local official skilled in calligraphy whose character was somewhat... [fragmentary]... mixed.
He was in a hurry to eat and did not have time to perform the ritual purification; he simply left the bowl as it was and departed. Consequently, his complexion became parched.

This man is still living, and the auspicious scripture [concerning this] also exists at Ximing Monastery in the capital, where the monastery director Shen Cha personally witnessed and described it (from the Fayuan zhulin).
Chan Master Shouchang respectfully examined the memorial: the Master’s name was Huìjīng; his style name was Wúmíng. He was the son of the Pèi family of Chóngrén, Fǔzhōu.

Initially, there were difficulties during his birth, but when his grandfather recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he was delivered safely. Consequently, he was named Jīng (Sūtra). From birth, he was exceptionally gifted and unlike his peers. His physical form...
His appearance was ancient and dignified, like a soaring crane ascending into the void. By nature he was serene and had no worldly attachments or preferences.
At the age of nine, upon entering the local school, he asked, "What is this 'vast and unyielding qi'? His teacher marveled at him.
Throughout his life, he appeared as if indifferent to the affairs of the human world. At seventeen, he abandoned his brush and inkstone, resolutely setting his mind on the Way. At twenty-one—

Once, while visiting the home of a lay devotee, he saw a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on a table. Upon reading it, he finished the entire scroll at once; he rejoiced as if he had recovered a long-lost possession.
He immediately explained his intention to the layman, who marveled at him. From that moment, the Master renounced meat and alcohol and resolved to leave the secular world.
His parents gave their consent. At that time, Chan Master Yun Kong Zhong was preaching the Dharma at Lingshan; the Master went there accordingly.
He relied upon him; thus, the Master’s original name was Huìjīng. He attended him for three years, never failing to follow his instructions with the humility of a fool.

He once harbored doubts regarding the four-line verse of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. One day, seeing a verse by Master Fǔ, he said: "If one discusses the four-line verse, it should not be separated from the body.
The Master suddenly felt a sense of clarity and composed a verse himself, which included the line: "Light radiates throughout the entire realm."
This phrase from the *Ming* [text] shows that it was awakened by the habitual cultivation of *prajñā* from former lives (from the *Shouchang Yulu*).
Gong Dezhuang,
a Proofreader at the Secretariat Library, having first been dismissed from office at Lingshou, returned to the capital and resided in a new [dwelling].
Inside the gate, at that time, Liu Yefu of Shandong—whose courtesy name was Fangshang—was on friendly terms with Dezhuang.

He had casually sent a short note inviting him to go and see the spectacle on the fourteenth day with his entire household, adding: "You must not go out; I wish to wait for you briefly to have a private conversation.
Dezhuang, who had always held the man in high esteem and respect, stayed alone guarding his dwelling until the second watch of the night, yet Yefu did not arrive. Just as he was about to...
He fell asleep while his family members had not yet returned. Suddenly, a fire broke out from the gate. Dezhuang merely grabbed the official decree and fled;

in a single night, several hundred households were reduced to ashes. The next day, he searched through the ashes and charcoal of the ruined houses and found a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

It was not damaged in the slightest; upon opening it for inspection, it appeared bright and fresh as if newly printed. Dezhuang had been a man of youthful luxury and indulgence, with a great fondness for wine.
Master Se did not have much faith in the Buddhist scriptures. Could it be that the inconceivable power of his roots of goodness from previous lives caused him to be moved by this realization?
The witnesses were Pengfan, Zou Zhengchen, Liu Fei, the monk Xizu, and Dehong.
The first day after the Lantern Festival of the first year of the Zhenghe era (as recorded in *Shimen Wenzichan*).

Zhou Jin of Hangzhou was a man of some learning who gathered two or three children to study together in the marketplace. He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day with great diligence.
One day, out of pity for a living creature, a child accidentally knocked over an oil lamp before the Buddha, and the oil stained the scripture. This was a common custom among the people of Hangzhou.

Whenever scriptures, images, or ritual cloths became soiled, they were habitually cast into the Tàojiāng River. Zhijin consequently bound them with red flames, following that precedent in his practice.
This was during the Gēnyí year (1300) of the Dàdé era of the Yuán dynasty. Three years later, in the Guīmǎo year (1303), the scriptures suddenly returned to their original location;
half of them were encased by tidal silt, yet the red flames remained as before. Zhijin was filled with wonder and joy, and together with the monk Jiǎnfú from Wúmén, he brushed away the debris.
The sand and dust were removed; those parts that were stuck together were carefully separated. He then requested eminent monks from various monasteries to provide inscriptions on the left side.
Eighty-one years later, in the *gengshen* year of the Hongwu era of our present dynasty, this scripture came into the hands of the śramaṇa Youdi, who once again had it bound and repaired.
He then invited Luo Lan of Mount Nanping to compose a eulogy, which reads as follows: [The eulogy follows.]
Sincerity moves all things; there is no gap between them even as fine as a hair or a speck of dust. This stimulus elicits that response, just as a magnet attracts a needle.

How much more so when one receives and upholds with a sincere heart the Sūtras spoken by the Hero of the World? The clear response is like an echo. Long ago, a man of the Zhou clan served [the Buddha] with solemnity morning and evening.
The sutra had been defiled and cast into the tides of the Yangtze River; after three years and four seasons, it suddenly returned to its original location.

Since the sutra was actually made of paper, it could hardly be compared to iron or stone; were it not for the power of the Vajra, how could it have remained undestroyed? The sutra had no wings or feet and could not fly.

It is not by the power of a diamond that it is brought here; by whom else could it have been carried? Judging from this, wherever the Buddha’s words reach, they are guarded by a hundred deities, and none can cause them harm.
Yet, as for this scripture, though it records the Buddha’s words by means of wooden slips and brushes, from where does its spiritual efficacy arise?
The Dharma-treasuries of the world and the scriptural texts they model fill the rafters and exhaust the cattle-stalls [of libraries], yet it has not been heard that all of them have been verified.

One should know that the myriad dharmas are in truth rooted in the single mind; because the mind is sincere, the scriptures respond to it. When the spirit of the mind and the spirit of the scriptures are one, there is no room for doubt regarding this principle.
Thus one knows that this mind is so vast it has no exterior, and so minute it has no interior. Its wondrous functions of spiritual penetration are each and every one fully complete;
there is no need to seek them elsewhere. If one can apply oneself with diligence, entering the Supreme Vehicle, there will be no obstacles to realizing the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment.
Now, by means of this praise of the sutra, I extend its meaning to reach you: for those who wish to become Buddhas, this very mind is it. Contemplate it well;
be careful not to regress. (From Song Jinglao’s *Record of Protecting the Dharma*)
The nun Jingzhen resided at Jixian Temple in Chang’an. She wore patched robes and lived by begging for alms. Throughout her life, she was free from anger.

She recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred thousand times and was single-mindedly devoted to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha. In the seventh month of the fifth year of the Xianqing era, she fell ill and said to her disciples:
Within five months, he beheld Amitābha Buddha ten times. Furthermore, on two occasions, he saw children playing upon jeweled lotus flowers in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
On five occasions, holy monks conferred upon him the prediction of enlightenment, saying, "You shall become a Buddha," and further declaring, "I have attained rebirth in the highest grade.
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. After one night had passed, he revived and said to his disciples, "I..."

He attained the rank of a bodhisattva and traveled throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas. Having finished speaking, he passed away, and his light illuminated the monastery (as recorded in the *Ruìyìng xiānchuán*).
The Woman of the Wang Family of Jixian, Song Dynasty. She recited daily the *Amitābha*, *Vajracchedikā*, and *Avalokiteśvara* sūtras, seeking deliverance through the practice of nianfo.
After her mother died and had been coffined, foul blood began to drip from the corpse. The woman made a vow, saying: "If my filial piety is sincere, may this stench not [spread]."

Having finished speaking, the flow of blood immediately ceased. His father took a second wife, and they together cultivated pure practices. Later, she fell ill and invited monks to explain the visualization methods of the Pure Land.
Suddenly, she asked for her robes and lay down in the auspicious posture. She grasped the hand of Avalokiteśvara; the banner she held remained perfectly still and motionless.
Her mother sifted ashes onto the ground to verify where she had been reborn, and saw several lotus flowers emerge from within the ashes.
Duo (from *Zhu Hong’s Collection on Rebirth*).

Huangpo of Chaoshan in the Song dynasty upheld the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras and focused her mind exclusively on the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, she contracted dysentery; she took only [rice water].
Shui bushi (Water-Not-Eating) was a monk from a neighboring hermitage who dreamed that a lay devotee came to him and said, "I am about to depart for the Western Land.
Two days later, the devotee faced west, recited the Buddha’s name, sat upright, and passed away. Those both near and far all saw red clouds covering the devotee’s dwelling.
(From *Zu Hong’s Collection on Rebirth*).
The layman Sun Dajian was the son of Sun Shuzi.
His dharma name was Dajian. From childhood, he was alert, quick-witted, upright, and resolute.

At the age of twelve, he accompanied his father, the layman Jingwu, to Yunqi Temple to pay homage to the image of Amitābha Buddha according to the Forty-eight Vows; thereupon, he received the five precepts and returned home.

He then abstained from meat and blood, ceased socializing, and abandoned his studies. Vowing to recite the Buddha’s name and pledging to attain the Golden Terrace, he practiced with such diligence that he disregarded even his own life.
Suddenly, he saw two bhikṣus holding lotus flowers, who confirmed his single-minded devotion to the Pure Land.
He further saw a transformed person reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for an entire day and night. Thereupon, he rose from his seat in a state of awe and said, "Amitābha..."
Avalokiteśvara came to welcome me from all sides. I formed the Great Vajra Fist Mudrā and called out the name of Amitābha Buddha several times;
then, I became still and tranquil. This was on the eleventh day of the eleventh month of the Xinhai year of the Wanli era.

There exists a "Song of the Twelve Hours of the Pure Land" that has been passed down through the ages, which is detailed in the biography of the Imperial Historian Wu Xisheng (contained in Zhuhong’s *Wangsheng ji*).
The "Vajra" in the title is a metaphor for that which is most firm and most sharp; it cannot be harmed by anything, yet it can destroy all things.
"Prajñā" is the Dharma, here translated as "wisdom. Wisdom possesses the function of discernment, while insight possesses the utility of illuminating and comprehending.

Furthermore, wisdom (*jñāna*) illuminates the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, while discerning insight (*prajñā*) realizes that all phenomena are unarisen. Nevertheless, they possess both essence and function. The *Treatise on the Ultimate Meaning* (*Zhao lun*) states:
"The true mark of all phenomena is called prajñā; it is the adamantine essence, firm. A sutra says: "When the mind of faith is pure, the true mark arises.
It further states: "To transform sentient beings is called upāya; it is the adamantine function, sharp. A sutra...
It is said: "I should bring all sentient beings to extinction, yet there is not a single sentient being who is actually extinguished.
It is further said: "Engaging with existence never begins with delusion regarding the void; therefore, one constantly dwells within existence without being defiled.

The Sūtra says: "One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on form; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental phenomena. It is also said: "One does not loathe existence while contemplating emptiness."

Therefore, one contemplates emptiness but does not realize it. As the Sūtra says: "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere. This means that apart from essence there is no function, and apart from function there is no essence.

By the power of a single thought-moment, both the provisional and the ultimate are simultaneously revealed. This is unlike the wisdom-eye of the emptiness of persons held by those of the Two Vehicles;
thus, it is metaphorically called the "Vajra Pāramitā. *Pāramitā* here translates as "reaching the other shore," which is a metaphor for the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa. If...
When there is the twofold grasping at a self and phenomena, there are the two kinds of birth and death: the fragmented and the transformational; these are called "this shore.
By boarding the vessel of Prajñā, one crosses the middle stream of self and phenomena, leaving behind this shore of the two kinds of birth and death to reach the other shore of Bodhi and Nirvāṇa;
therefore, it is named *pāramitā*. Question: True Prajñā is pure like space.

Emptiness is without cognition or vision, without action or conditions. Now that Śākyamuni has appeared in the world to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings, he causes them to leave behind the notions of self and dharmas, to sever birth and death, to cultivate *prajñā*, and to realize *nirvāṇa*.

Yet, once the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, then all things—ordinary and holy, subject and object, arising and ceasing, cultivation and realization—are merely deluded sentiments. How, then, can they be called true *prajñā*? He replied:
This is not so. The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to objects, like the moon reflected in water.

When the water is clear, the moon appears, yet the moon does not come; when the water is turbid, the moon is obscured, yet the moon does not go away. As a sutra says: "The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks.
Thus, the responsive and transformational bodies are not the ultimate reality. Furthermore, it says: "Suppose there is a person whose body is like..."
The Buddha taught that Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is not a body; this is called the "Great Body. This *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) is unattainable. Furthermore, it is said:
"There is not even the slightest dharma that can be attained; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This *dharmakāya* (dharma body) is non-attainable.
Since the Buddha has no attainment, how could the Dharma be expounded? Therefore, when the World-Honored One preached the sutras three times...
Throughout more than a hundred assemblies and for forty-nine years preaching the Dharma, he never spoke a single word. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"The Wheel of Dharma was turned three times throughout the great trichiliocosm, yet that wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure. A sūtra further states: "If one perceives the Tathāgata as having preached any dharma, one slanders the Buddha;
that there is no dharma to be preached is itself called 'preaching the Dharma. Since it is thus with the transformer, so too is it with those transformed.
It is likewise so. Since afflictions are fundamentally empty, how could there be a self or dharmas? As neither of these two attachments exists, what need is there to eliminate them?
They are as unreal in name and substance as a rabbit’s horn or a tortoise’s hair. As the Sūtra says: "The mark of a self is precisely no-mark;

the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are precisely no-marks. What is called the mark of dharmas, the Tathāgata says, is precisely not the mark of dharmas. This is an analogy.

Like an illusion or a cataract, one falsely perceives flowers in the sky. If the cataract is removed, how could the flowers in the sky exist? Sentient beings, through the delusions of affliction, falsely perceive birth and death.
If afflictions are eliminated, where would birth and death abide? Just as when the skin no longer exists, what can the hair attach itself to? The *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says:
"Birth and death, nirvana, ordinary people, and all Buddhas—all are equally the appearance of flowers in the sky. A sutra states: "One..."
All sentient beings are, in truth, not sentient beings. My Dharma is the object illuminated; Prajñā is the mind that illuminates.
Since my Dharma is fundamentally empty, who is there to be illuminated? As there is no object to be illuminated, there is no mind capable of illuminating.
When both subject and object are forgotten, cultivation is itself non-cultivation. As the Sūtra says: "Because there is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span."

Birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa are both terms of relative opposition. Nevertheless, to say that one attains bodhi by leaving behind afflictions (*kleśa*), or that one realizes nirvāṇa by severing birth-and-death, is speech conforming to the intentions of others;
it is not the Tathāgata’s discourse in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*).

When illuminated by the wisdom of *prajñā*, afflictions are fundamentally empty—how could there be bodhi? Birth-and-death is originally quiescent—where could nirvāṇa be lodged? As the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* says:

Prajñā is the wisdom that realizes [this], and nirvana is the principle realized. When cultivation is itself non-cultivation, then there is no one who [cultivates].
The wisdom that realizes [this] is itself non-realization; thus, there is no principle of an object to be realized. Forgetting the subject and object, and extinguishing mental images, Panshan said:

Having completed his transformative work, he entered extinction and returned to the truth, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is spent. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "If one sees that the Tathāgata is eternally present..."
It does not perish. [Sentient beings] are unable to conceive the thought that it is difficult to encounter, nor do they give rise to a heart of reverence.

This means that extinction is such that there is nothing to be extinguished. Thus, Nirvāṇa is empty and without marks; Prajñā is quiescent and without cognition.
Fundamentally, there is no birth-and-death or arising-and-ceasing, nor is there affliction, bondage, or liberation.
By means of suchness-wisdom, one accords with the principle of suchness. Outside of this principle there is no wisdom; outside of wisdom there is no principle.
When both wisdom and principle are simultaneously extinguished, they transcend both speech and thought. This is why Śākyamuni closed his room in Magadha and Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī;

why Subhūti sat peacefully in meditation amidst the crags and Śakra filled the sky with falling flowers. How could it be said that there was no eloquence? It is simply that there is nothing which eloquence can express.

Regarding the miraculous efficacy of the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra* as transmitted throughout ancient and modern times in both China and Japan—how could it possibly be fully recorded upon every hair’s breadth of paper?
Now, as for the responses to the influence of harmony in the present age, let us set aside those scattered throughout various books.

I shall record here, as they come to hand, whatever I have encountered within the texts of foreign lands—without distinguishing between monastics and laypeople, and regardless of chronological order—and title this work *The Record of Miraculous Responses to the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
This is because it shares commonalities with the *Record of Resonant Responses* (*Ganying zhuan*) and the *New Records of the Extraordinary*.
This record has been compiled and carved into printing blocks to be bequeathed to like-minded companions of the world.
